articles.text: Piedmont elementary schools will not reopen November 3rd; the return of kids to in-person learning has been rescheduled for Tuesday, December 1st for TK-2 grade and December 8th for grades 3-5. According to School Superintendent Randy Booker, the delay was due to the district’s inability to create a master school schedule for the three elementary schools. Teachers opting out of in-person teaching or resigning has left the district short on teachers. A total of 74 percent of parents chose in-person learning for their elementary school students, while 26 percent preferred to stay with distance learning. Parent surveys were sent on October 9 and received back by October 14. In an email sent to parents on October 23, Booker stated, “Based on criteria spelled-out in our agreements with staff, teacher assignment has become even more complicated... especially with a desire to minimize involuntary transfers of our educators from one site to another, or even from grade level to grade level.” In the school board meeting Booker said the number of teachers that need to be hired is “less than a handful.” The exact number of teachers that need to be hired has not been publicly disclosed. For over 50 years, the Scouts have cheerfully procured, sold, trimmed and delivered all your favorite conifers from Silver Tip to Noble and Douglas Firs. Sales will commence November 1 and will be exclusively online at www.scouttreelot.org. A limited option to purchase by phone will be available for customers who do not have online access. The purpose of all Piedmont BSA Scout programs is to “Prepare for Life” or to prepare Piedmont youth for whatever life brings. By Betsy Smegal Andersen There is no question the Piedmont Community Pool is on track for permanent closure. So, let’s pause for a moment and picture Piedmont without a pool. Without a local pool, Piedmonters won’t have a place to gather together in the center of town, fostering friendships while their children learn to swim and play, or exercising themselves before or after a long day’s work. Instead, residents will be scattered across the East Bay, in search of affordable pool time. Sure, some families will get on lists for limited spots at private clubs, but for most residents, the cost of joining a private club, along with the monthly dues and the travel time, is not a feasible option. East Bay swim teams will continue to exist, but there would be no more “Piedmont” swim team. Or go to piedmontpost.org/subscribe. OPINIONtown for all practices and competitions, with carpools, rental fees, and late-night practices far away from home. Can you imagine if we made our high school football team do that? Or our basketball or tennis teams? Without our local pool, there will be no summer jobs for our young adults to teach swim classes or lifeguard. There will be no water aerobics, no lap swim, no recreational play or swim camps, and no local swim lessons. Instead of a pool, we will have a big empty hole in the center of town. And then what? We don’t have to imagine a future without a pool much longer – it is our reality. I believe Piedmont voters want to live in a town that provides welcoming civic spaces for all to enjoy – parks, playfields, and yes, a safe and accessible pool facility. Instead of facing a future without a local pool, let’s come together, build community, and invest in the future of Piedmont. Please join my family and me in voting Yes on Measure UU. articles.text: Cooper’s proven commitment to schools Editor: Based on my experiences working closely with Hilary Cooper on several campaigns for the Piedmont schools, I believe that Hilary would be an excellent school board member. Hilary has proven her commitment to our schools by volunteering for important roles over the past 11 years, including parent club president at PMS and PHS, Spring Fling co-chair, Giving Campaign co-chair (twice), and co-chair of the campaign to pass Measures G&H. I can vouch for Hilary’s capabilities because I worked alongside her, and former school board member Doug Ireland, last fall to co-chair the successful campaign to pass Measures G&H, our very important school parcel taxes. Hilary is one of those rare leaders who is good at both the big picture of strategy and the heavy lifting of day-to-day volunteering. During the campaign, Hilary had great ideas about how to promote and explain the parcel taxes, and she was willing and able to do the work behind the scenes, including endless emails, phone calls and spreadsheets. When Hilary decided to run for school board, I happily volunteered to be her campaign manager. I believe that one of the most important things we can do to support our schools this fall (in addition to donating to the Giving Campaign) is to elect a capable school board. During this campaign, Hilary has continued to work hard to learn even more about the latest ideas in education, including how to bring our students and teachers back to school safely. Hilary does her homework by reading, talking to experts, and thinking about the issues. Hilary’s most important qualification for school board is her leadership style. She listens with an open mind, carefully considers the issues, makes decisions, and then takes action. She handles challenging situations with an impressive balance of gravitas and optimism. As the parent of two children at Piedmont Middle School, I care about the future of our schools. I know that Hilary would not just settle for the “new normal,” instead she would help us make our schools even better. She would advocate for all students, and she would make sure that all voices in our
articles.title: Candidate Letters Main

articles.text: Editor: I am writing in full support of Jen Cavenaugh’s campaign for re-election to the Piedmont City Council. We met in 2011 when I was new to the city and our children attended Beach Elementary together. Over the past three years, I have gotten to know Jen better, both professionally and personally, through PADC (Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee). She is a strong advocate for inclusivity and truly listens to the perspectives of all stakeholders. Her ability to build rapport, make strong connections, skillfully collaborate, and take action make her an ideal thought partner between the city and community members. Her experience and background in management and business has proven to be an asset to the city and her deep understanding of fiduciary and fiscal responsibilities benefit both the city and the residents of Piedmont. Her track record as an active volunteer and as a current City Council member speaks to her level of dedication and commitment to public service. She will continue to serve the city well as a leader with integrity. I urge you to vote for Jen for re-election to the Piedmont City Council.
articles.title: Cavenaugh listens to perspectives of all stakeholders

articles.text: Editor: I met Cory Smegal in 2009 when we were co-presidents of our respective elementary school parent clubs. Since those early days, I’ve watched as Cory has consistently taken on new and increasingly significant roles to support our students and district. In addition, now I’m privileged to call her my friend. I again worked closely with Cory last year when I was president of PHS Parents’ Club. Cory was always a supportive and active School Board member, even before COVID turned things upside-down. One attribute I respect about Cory is that she always anchors her positions and efforts on what’s best for students. During her term she has led our district’s efforts to advocate for children across the state. In this way, she helps Piedmont take a leadership role in ensuring quality education for all. The traits that make Cory a great friend also make her a great community leader. She listens, is responsive, and works hard. She’s thoughtful, balanced and researches her positions before she reaches conclusions. And Cory is pragmatic, with a strong sense of fiduciary responsibility. Mostly, Cory cares deeply for our town and its children. Please join me in re-electing Cory Smegal for School Board. –Laura Katter the community. She understands the challenges all parents are facing. Veronica is a collaborator who will work well with others, listen to what the pain points are and then create a plan to solve those issues. Veronica is not an establishment candidate. Her perspective with identifying the needs of the community and putting in a plan to address those needs will benefit our schools. She will be a voice for teachers, parents and students in our community. She will look at problems through an equity lens and continue to drive the academic excellence that Piedmont is known for. Join me this November in voting for Veronica Anderson Thigpen as a member of the Piedmont School Board.
articles.title: Smegal – caring for her town and its children

articles.text: Editor: I am writing to express my enthusiastic and informed support for the candidacy of Hilary Cooper for PUSD’s School Board in our election coming up November 3rd. Through my work with Hilary on both the Piedmont Ed Foundation and campaigns for measures G & H, I have seen first-hand that she possesses the experience, perspective and ability that will be crucial as our district weathers the unique challenges 2020 has presented us in maintaining our academic excellence, while keeping our students, teachers and administrators safe. Experience: What comes to mind most is her work on the Giving Campaign as she was able to build on prior efforts and create an organized, unified “ask” that helped generate significant lift in overall community contributions as we merged the parent board and PEF campaigns. Perspective: As someone who has been a teacher, parent and volunteer within PUSD, she has institutional knowledge from all angles that will help her make the “right calls” for all constituents in our school community. Ability: As a community member said to me on hearing of Hilary’s candidacy, “She gets things done. Full stop.” Brynne and I moved here 23 years ago so our kids could have an experience that is too rare in the Bay Area these days; a chance for them to live near their school friends while benefiting from a community commitment to education that is second to none. I am confident that Hilary will do us “Did Dude touch the shredder button while I was leaning over my waste basket?”
articles.title: Cooper’s experience, perspective will aid school board

articles.text: Editor: I am endorsing Veronica Anderson Thigpen for school board. My family and I moved to Piedmont over a year ago. articles.text: Sales from vendors on Piedmont’s public sidewalks and in parks will be allowed as of Wednesday, November 4. Interested vendors will have to apply for a permit with the Piedmont Police Department. Vending in parks will only be permitted on paved areas and pedestrian movement cannot be impeded. The second reading of the ordinance was approved by City Council on Monday, October 5. After some discussion, a first reading was unanimously approved by Council on September 21. The ordinance brings Piedmont’s laws into compliance with new state legislation. On January 1, 2019, Senate Bill 946 established statewide rules for permitting vending on sidewalks and parks. The goal of the bill, signed by former Governor Jerry Brown in 2018, was to make the process less onerous for vendors. “The bill states that its purpose is to promote entrepreneurship and support immigrant and low-income communities, by decriminalizing the selling of food and merchandise on public sidewalks and in parks statewide,” Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, who has spearheaded the new sidewalk vending permitting process in the City, told the Post. The City defines a sidewalk vendor as a vendor selling food, beverages or merchandise by hand or from a non-motorized cart, wagon or rack. A vendor can be either roaming or stationary, although a stationary vendor cannot set up shop in a residential zone. “[SB 946] requires that cities allow sidewalk vending, and restrictions may only be imposed when directly related to objective public health, safety or welfare concerns,” Bowers continued. “Local jurisdictions that wish to regulate sidewalk vending are required to first adopt a compliant program with rules and regulations consistent with SB 946.” To receive a permit applicants need to provide personal identification, list the items intended for sale and undergo criminal background checks. Applicants must also submit evidence of health permits for food vending and state seller’s permits, as required. Bowers said that approval of applications will likely take 3-5 days, so applicants won’t be able to submit a permit and begin selling the same day. PPD will send notification to applicants regarding the decisions. SB 946 says there can be no limit to the number of sidewalk vendor permits issued. Approval or denial will hinge “on the basis of the ordinance requirements for the application and after an assessment of the individual’s criminal history, if one exists,” Bowers explained. Historically, the City has not allowed vendors on sidewalks or parks. The City Code does not explicitly regulate sidewalk vending, Bowers said. The City Attorney and PPD worked alongside the Planning Department and Recreation Department in crafting the new regulations. Vending may be prohibited under certain circumstances, such as if a vendor impedes movement on a sidewalk or if a special event is taking place. The City still does not allow food trucks. More information can be found on the City’s website.
articles.title: New city ordinance complies with state law

articles.text: Energy Reach Codes have the potential to change how the city functions in the future. As an employee with the City’s Planning Department, I would like to explain how they function and how they started. The California Energy Commission is a government organization that wants to ensure that California energy is clean and efficient now and in the future. The commission determines every three years to make sure cities have standards for energy efficiency. The subject may sound dry, but these energy code updates can change how we create buildings and infrastructure throughout the entire state. Once the state agency dictates standards, it is up to local municipalities to enact them and make sure that buildings are code compliant. Sometimes municipalities choose to go beyond what is currently required. This is when “reach codes” come into play. These proposals “reach” further than the existing energy codes, and help municipalities become more efficient than the state mandates. But Reach codes can be a tricky policy to pass. Because the state has new guidelines every three years, municipalities run the risk of having their reach codes become redundant when the next code cycle comes around. For example, the new set of statewide codes will become standard in 2023. However, municipalities don’t want to go too far, as this would leave both residents and contractors frustrated with changes that could feel too heavy-handed. When passing Reach codes, it’s critical to achieve balance: something that residents feel is reasonable and will be approved by City Council, and something that is still valid in three years. Piedmont is in the midst of a Reach code effort. The City is attempting to create a revised Reach code that will drastically cut greenhouse gas emissions from residences. If you are interested in learning about the different perspectives on this Reach code, there are numerous articles in the local papers, as well as on the City website. The City webpage has a FAQ section designed to answer many of the more common questions. Reach codes are common throughout the state, and a pretty good way to bring about changes. It’s an interesting experiment that other cities can look at to determine if a particular code is worth pursuing or not. It allows cities with more resources to attempt more solutions to their energy issues, while cities with fewer resources can pass codes that other cities have adopted, or wait for the three-year state cycle to come around again. For example, Piedmont’s Reach code was partially inspired by Berkeley’s first-in-the-nation ban on gas in new buildings. This kind of “observation before adoption” can make Reach codes a unique way to attempt new ordinances and be environmentally friendly pioneers. Piedmont’s attempts to pass Reach codes showcase some of the leadership for which this community is known. Piedmont is #1 in median family income, #6 in median household income, and #14 in per capita income in the state, so it makes sense for us to be at the forefront of environmental work. The proposed Reach codes is a way for equitable changes to be made in the building sector. Nate Redinbo is an Americorps fellow working this year in the City of Piedmont’s Planning and Building Department. Contact him at nredinbo@piedmont.ca.gov with any opinions and questions on reach codes, jogging, or bread baking. He will be publishing a monthly article on environmental topics that affect Piedmonters.
articles.title: What exactly are Reach Codes?

articles.text: Piedmont will kick off its second annual citywide Climate Challenge next month, following the success of its first challenge in 2019-2020. Last year, over 250 Piedmont households answered the call to be more environmentally-conscience through different challenges that aimed to reduce the city’s collective greenhouse gas emissions by over 200 tons. The city has announced an intention to double the number of participant households from 250 to 500 sign-ups by Earth Day, April 22, 2021. In addition, a goal has been set to reduce Piedmont’s carbon emissions by 500 tons. The Climate Challenge gives residents the chance to participate in teams and community organizations and to engage in some friendly competition to see which household can reduce their carbon footprint the most. Residents can use the platform to learn more about their household’s emissions and to plan lifestyle changes that will positively affect their impact on the environment. The challenge divides actionbased difficulty, from installing solar panels on houses, to switching to an electric vehicle, to turning off the water while brushing teeth. A new category, “Hanging out at home,” has been added given the number of people sheltering in place. Actions in this category are geared toward those who are telecommuting to work and spending most of their time in their home due to Covid- 19 health restrictions. The city is encouraging residents who signed up for the challenge last year to continue to participate. New challenges have been added. The Climate Challenge will go from November 2020 to May 2021. Sign up for the challenge at https://www.piedmontclimatechallenge.org/. There, you will create a profile for your household, and pledge to commit to adopt sustainable actions that help reduce your carbon footprint. Those actions will be added to your dashboard, and the platform will help with next steps, costs, and questions. “This is a fun, meaningful way to work towards a shared decrease in Piedmont emissions. Households, household transit and household consumption are responsible for more emissions than municipal or commercial activities combined. Using this website brings attention to this fact. It helps us all be more sustainable,” said Climate Fellow Nate Redinbo.
articles.title: Piedmont doubles its goals for this year’s Climate Challenge

articles.text: What do you see in this Rorschach image? I am the Head of a small independent high school and, to be honest, the last seven months have been brutal. And there’s no end in sight. We might go back to school at some point, in some form, but nothing’s going to feel normal, at least not anytime soon. Here’s how I deal with it. Every day I write an email to my school community. It’s called Sue’s Spew. I compose it in the dialect of adolescence, which is sarcasm, and so the thing pretty much writes itself. All I need is a little input from the community and I have my fodder for the day. For instance, last week I gave them a Rorschach image (I’m teaching Psychology and we are studying projective tests). I asked the community to tell me what they saw in the image. I may make this a regular feature of the Spew because I got mountains of stuff, which I then wrote about in my next Spew. People were seeing gnomes, and rhinos, and rhinos on acid . . . it was great. Another time I asked people to share their most recent rabbit hole experiences (mine was aliens) and I got a wealth of material. From the origin of language to Magyarization to Schitt’s Creek, you wouldn’t believe the stuff they came up with. Now this is parents, too – no kid is researching Magyarization, I can tell you. But this is what makes the Spew great – it’s a family affair. I also try to get serious (because, well, I’m the Head of School), and so I have features such as Wise Words Wednesdays. I can’t go too deep otherwise I’ll lose my audience. Teenagers have about a 90-second tolerance for sincerity before they tune out, and actually that’s being generous. So, I Spew away, and I try to get as many people involved as possible. I have my regular readers, such as Alessandro (his real name), who proposed last week – in response to the Rorschach image – that I should let him run the school. Believe me, I’m tempted. I started the Spew on March 12, the day we went online, but back then I didn’t call it the Spew. I sure as heck didn’t think it would last this long. But here we are. Trying to stay connected as a community. Trying to stay positive. Trying ... just to survive. And so, I spew. I highly recommend it. In non-pandemic time if the AQI surpasses 200 (very unhealthy), “the Superintendent shall confer with the Board of Education and the Superintendent for the Alameda County Office of Education to determine if a school closure is warranted,” the policy states. AQI measures six air pollutants: PM2.5 (particulate matter with a diameter less than 2.5 micrometers), PM10, ozone, carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide. During the COVID-19 pandemic the cut off limit will be 101 AQI (unhealthy for sensitive groups). All classes will be canceled ahead of time if the forecast is for 101 AQI or above. In-person learning is predicated upon having a high level of air circulation. Running school ventilation systems during days with large amounts of particulate in the air would rapidly clog the newly installed MERV-13 filters. The MERV-13 filters are a requirement for schools to be able to open. Superintendent Randy Booker explained that the filters are not only expensive, but difficult to procure at this time. During COVID-19, if the AQI gets to 101 or higher unexpectedly during the school day, and if the ventilation is shut off, school will be canceled for the day. articles.text: Ever since Disney princesses have been created, everyone around the world has loved them. There have been Disney-themed birthdays, millions of people have packed Disneyland parks, and even more continue to buy Disney Princess merchandise. But recently some people have decided to “cancel” them, claiming that something is offensive and therefore the Disney Princess products should not be sold. So, what’s the trouble with Disney princesses – Belle, Rapunzel or Aurora? People are saying that they’re too unrealistic, that their body types and their beauty is not something that children should strive to emulate. I agree, but Disney characters by definition are fantasy and never meant to be something people should strive to achieve. Nor are they the world’s standard of beauty. They’re entertainment, just like fairy tales they represent. Entertainment follows some simple rules: it has to give people joy, make them laugh, make them have a good time. A Disney Princess technically isn’t even a real princess. In their fantasy world, being a princess is just doing what they want without any duties. But being a real royal is much harder. Take the Queen of England for example. She doesn’t spend all her time planning parties and hanging out with her friends. She actually has to run a whole country. She has to discuss policies with her parliament, implement new rules, meet dignitaries. When the creators of Disney Princesses were brainstorming what their characters would represent, I’m quite sure it wasn’t real royalty. People are also saying that the Disney Princesses lack diversity. This is wrong on many levels and shows ignorance. There are many different cultures, ethnicities and backgrounds among Disney princesses. For example, there is Princess Jasmine of Saudi Arabia, Princess Anastasia of Russia, Princess Tiana of New Orleans, who is African-American, Merida of Scotland, and Pocahontas, a Native American. And then there’s Ariel, who is half-fish. Yes, the Disney organization has had its problems with diversity, but they are demonstrating that any culture or ethnicity can be a princess. Not that everything is flawless in the Disney universe. Disney recently released the live action Mulan on the Disney Plus channel. Mulan is a Chinese princess, so Disney filmed parts of it in China. Some scenes were shot in the province where Uigher Muslims, a local oppressed minority, had been forced into internment camps. (China continues to deny the existence of these camps). That caused rightful criticism from human rights advocates around the world. The lead actress Liu Yifei spoke out in support of the police in Hong Kong, despite the fact the police were using excessive force and violence against the pro-democracy protesters. So, Disney could have done a better job. And it doesn’t help the Disney image to see some poor production decisions. Mushu, the beloved small red dragon from the Mulan animation, is missing in the live action version. And there is no singing and no love interest. But does a problem with one particular movie mean we should “cancel” the entire franchise? I don’t think so. Cancel culture, of course, isn’t just the Disney Princess problem. People are “canceling” movies, other people, songs, basically anything that they deem unfit or offensive for today’s world. Anybody can get “cancelled” at any moment. It got so bad that former President Barack Obama recently called attention to the cancel culture. In a video, he said, “That’s not activism. If all you’re doing is casting stones, then that’s probably not going to get you very far.” I agree: if you tell everyone what they are doing is wrong, that’s not going to create change. Instead, we should openly discuss important issues. We should learn to listen, not just to shut down. I grew up with the Disney Princesses. When I was a kid I would watch princess movies and I wanted to be just like them, which for me meant running through the forest, meeting Prince Charming, and having flawless hair in the morning, I did want all that, but I never thought that I had to look like them, or that I had to be perfect in every way. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: The time is Now for Measure UU Our kids are grown, we don’t swim often, and we are 100% in support of Measure UU. Twenty-three years ago, when we moved to Piedmont with two young boys and a daughter on the way, there was a pool for us because caring people decades earlier had built it. Like most young families we couldn’t afford a private club and we didn’t have enough hours in the day to drive to other towns. The Piedmont pool taught our kids to swim, introduced us to our neighbors and lifelong friends, and provided cool relief on hot nights. It was a gift that Piedmonters whose kids were long grown had given to us. Now we’re thankful for the chance to pay it forward. The time is right for Measure UU. Our 56-year-old pool is no longer viable. It is no longer functional, and it is decades out of date for competitive swimming, water polo, and recreational sports. If we leave it empty, we deprive today’s families and athletes of an asset we’ve all had the opportunity to enjoy. And if there were ever a moment to take a pool off-line and rebuild it with minimal disruption, it is right now when a global pandemic restricts most swimming anyway. We can build something for the next 50 years now and give everyone in Piedmont a better place to gather when this sad and lonely time ends. So whether you ever expect to use the Piedmont pool or not, please vote for Measure UU. A community is more than just people who live in the same space; it’s a space where people look out for one another. Today, our home is literally surrounded by families with young children. They’ve settled here because generations of Piedmonters before them invested in families yet to come. These families make our lives richer (and our homes more valuable). It’s one of the strange joys of living in a place like this that whenever you do something good for others, you somehow find it does something good for you, too. A new pool helps all of us. Please join us in voting Yes on Measure UU to invest in a healthy Piedmont. get, and then hire the appropriate designers, contractors and other experts to bring your ideas to reality. If the community can first agree on the need for a new pool to replace the now defunct facility, then Measure UU authorizes up to $19.5 million which will be overseen by a committee and issued based on the final design. Setting a bond limit now and having each household pay for the bond issue is appropriate. I would submit that construction of a beautiful, new, public pool facility in Piedmont in return for a bond issue that costs less than the price of a Starbucks Venti Latte per week, per household, is an affordable and not unreasonable price for Piedmont residents to bear. Please join me in support of Measure UU. We can come together as a community and replace this deteriorated aquatics facility with a new pool facility for future generations to enjoy.
articles.title: Poll Letters Main

articles.text: What is Measure UU? Measure UU is a local Bond Measure which will provide funds to construct a safe, sustainable, and affordable community pool for Piedmont families, students, and adults of all ages. Why is Measure UU needed? Built in 1964, the Piedmont Community Pool is well past the end of its useful life and needs to be replaced. Not only are there serious safety issues (on more than one occasion the concrete deck has failed and crumbled into the pool), the locker room facilities are outdated and restrooms do not comply with the Americans with Disability Act (ADA) requirements, the decades-old plumbing is failing and the pool leaks approximately 3,000 gallons of water daily – over a million gallons a year. Without the Piedmont Community Pool, Piedmont would be the only city (and only public school district) in Alameda County without access to a local pool. What will Measure UU funds do? The successful passage of Measure UU ensures that the Piedmont community will continue to have its own local pool facility for school sports/PE programs, lessons, and recreation, for the next 50 years. The cost includes planning, architectural fees, legal fees, demolition and construction for two new pools, restrooms, locker rooms, and community space. The three existing pools will be replaced with two pools to meet resident needs: a warmer recreation pool with areas for safe water play, swim lessons, therapeutic swim, and physical rehabilitation; and a wider and deeper pool for recreation, physical education, water aerobics, water polo, swim team, and lap swimming. How much will Measure UU cost? Measure UU would allow the City to issue up to $19.5M in 30-year fixed rate bonds. Measure UU will cost 2.6 cents per $100 of assessed home value (NOT market rate value). For the median Piedmont home, this works out to less than 75 cents a day. To look up your assessed value, use this link to the Alameda County Assessor’s Office and enter your address: http://acgov. org/MS/prop/index.aspx What happens if Measure UU does not pass? When the 56-year-old Piedmont Pool is permanently closed, there will be no local swimming pool for residents or for Piedmont students. Piedmonters will have to travel and pay to use other communities’ pools, or pay initiation fees and annual dues for private swim clubs. With an empty padlocked pool facility in the center of town, the City will then have to decide what to do with that space. It is important to note that while the City decides, there is a cost to securing the site from blight and vandalism, as well as a significant cost associated with any future use of that space, whether it be for a pool or for some other use. If Measure UU passes, will there be a membership fee to use the pool? No, there is no membership fee. The Piedmont Community Pool has been a public pool since 2011. If Measure UU passes, the municipal bonds will be used to rebuild the pool facility. When the new facility opens, pool users will pay daily use fees, camp and lesson fees, annual and seasonal passes, and facility rentals, to offset operating costs. Pools are different from tennis courts and playing fields (which the City pays to maintain) in that pools are required to have trained staff present on-site during hours of operation (e.g. lifeguards, janitorial services). Like all programs run through the Recreation Department, Piedmont residents will have priority and will pay lower use fees than non-residents. For additional information visit the City of Piedmont’s website and FAQ page: https://piedmont.ca.gov/services___ departments/city_clerk/elections/november_3_2020_general_municipal_election/transfer_tax__pool_bond_measures/ pool_bond_frequently_asked_questions More information is also available at: www.communitypoolforpiedmont.com community life for many; a place where they see friends, meet neighbors, and hold celebrations. The project would include restrooms accessible to users of the adjacent Corey Reich Tennis Center, which currently has no restroom access. This would be a significant improvement to another popular community recreational facility. The pool isn’t the only infrastructure in Piedmont that will need attention in the coming years, and it might be more convenient if we didn’t need to address the pool now. However, it will not get less expensive with time, and, with the extraordinarily low interest rates expected to be in place for the next few years, this is actually the most opportune time to build it. Besides, the state of the current pool is such that it is unlikely to be reopened, as the rates of breakdown, mechanical failures, and leakage have made it no longer feasible to operate. The alternative scenario of a facility chained and closed for an indefinite duration is not, in our opinion, acceptable for a community the caliber of Piedmont. There will likely be more bond measures for other community facilities on the ballot in the coming years. Like all of us, we wish these things were less expensive. But we also think that we have all benefitted from capital investments made by generations past, and we think it is upon us now to make capital

articles.text: The November 2016 pool study on which Measure UU is based did not take into account the City Climate Action Plan. It called for a pool three times larger than the existing one. I believe that a larger pool could meet the CAB goal if about 150 households committed to installing solar panels on their houses and to assign the energy generated to the City. The current pool energy bill per year is $60,000. At $1.61 per therm it uses 37,267 therms per year. One therm equals 29.3 kWh. Hence 37,267 therms equals 1,091,925 kWh. Let us assume that because of a better design, the proposed pool would need twice rather than three times as much heat energy. One house with 8 panels produces 4,800 kWh. Therefore 454 houses would generate enough electricity to heat the new pool. Given the efficiency factor of three between electric energy and natural gas to generate heat , 454/3 or about 150 houses would be enough (this holds whether the pool uses a natural gas heat exchanger or heat pumps, as natural gas power plants are about 33% efficient to convert natural gas into electricity due to Carnot). The City would be ahead by 37,267 therms per year, thereby also making progress towards the long term 2050 CAB goal. As far as I understand in this forum and others, the proponents of Measure UU have committed to constrain the size of the pool so that it meets the City CAB, and to only issue the proportion of the Measure UU bond adjusted to the pool size compatible with the CAB. Under these conditions, I support Measure UU. I do think that the calculations are correct as the proposed number of houses is certainly in the right order of magnitude.
articles.title: Measure UU can fit in City’s Climate Action

articles.text: Editor: As Piedmont homeowners, our family advocates in favor of Measure UU even though we: 1) have never visited the pool 2) may not use the new pool and 3) are generally opposed to regressive taxes. Why then am I in favor of UU? It’s not because the pool is leaking 3,000 gallons per day and needs to be fixed, or because the increased tax will have a limited impact on our finances at only $30/month (which is well above the average amount for homeowners since we recently purchased our house). Nor is it because I think the initiative is infallibly written. Rather, it is because of the decision we made to live in Piedmont when we relocated from the East Coast four years ago. We seriously considered all of the more affordable surrounding cities, but Piedmont prevailed because of the quality of its schools and, equally as important, its real sense of community. I’ve built my community by taking leadership roles on the boards of the Havens Dads Club and Piedmont Baseball and Softball Foundation, and by coaching the many sports teams that both my elementary school boys are on. So, even though we’re not a “swimming family,” I still believe that Piedmont families who seek community at the pool should have a great facility. Piedmont has invested significantly in the many sports fields and parks that all children and adults in the community enjoy. Those fields are part of the reason that Piedmont is as amazing as it is, and it would be even more so with an updated pool and facility to bring the community together. The ballot initiative isn’t perfect, nor is the timing of raising taxes during a pandemic, but rarely are plans in life perfect. Perfect should not be the enemy of the good. Vote Yes on UU to bring our neighborhoods even closer together at a time when our strong community is more important than ever.
articles.title: Former East Coast residents say Yes to a new pool

articles.text: In this country and in this city, in particular, there is a significant discrepancy between the amount of money spent on private vs. public improvements. The current situation – crumbling public infrastructure – is the result of years of the community’s inability to fully commit to supporting our public facilities. I see Measure UU to rebuild the Piedmont Community Pool first and foremost as a simple question: whether we, as a community, value a pool or not? City public improvements such as pools, parks, courts, tracks, and trails are the last remaining vestiges of what can be considered the commons – outdoor places that play a central role in both creating community and providing for the simple, nearby enjoyment of the outdoors. In an urban context, we would do well to not let our lives be limited to the experience of individual spaces, such as our cars or our homes. If we let our lives be connected only virtually by digital technologies, we lose out in the richness of experience that our world has to offer. pages.text: 10 Wednesday, October 28, 2020 Poll Letters Main The time is Now for Measure UU By Jeff and Becky Bleich Our kids are grown, we don’t swim often, and we are 100% in support of Measure UU. Twenty-three years ago, when we moved to Piedmont with two young boys and a daughter on the way, there was a pool for us because caring people decades earlier had built it. Like most young families we couldn’t afford a private club and we didn’t have enough hours in the day to drive to other towns. The Piedmont pool taught our kids to swim, introduced us to our neighbors and lifelong friends, and provided cool relief on hot nights. It was a gift that Piedmonters whose kids were long grown had given to us. Now we’re thankful for the chance to pay it forward. The time is right for Measure UU. Our 56-year-old pool is no longer viable. It is no longer functional, and it is decades out of date for competitive swimming, water polo, and recreational sports. If we leave it empty, we deprive today’s families and athletes of an asset we’ve all had the opportunity to enjoy. And if there were ever a moment to take a pool off-line and rebuild it with minimal disruption, it is right now when a global pandemic restricts most swimming anyway. We can build something for the next 50 years now and give everyone in Piedmont a better place to gather when this sad and lonely time ends. So whether you ever expect to use the Piedmont pool or not, please vote for Measure UU. A community is more than just people who live in the same space; it’s a space where people look out for one another. Today, our home is literally surrounded by families with young children. They’ve settled here because generations of Piedmonters before them invested in families yet to come. These families make our lives richer (and our homes more valuable). It’s one of the strange joys of living in a place like this that whenever you do something good for others, you somehow find it does something good for you, too. A new pool helps all of us. Please join us in voting Yes on Measure UU to invest in a healthy Piedmont. remodel before you decide as a household that you need a new bathroom? Certainly not. You assess the problem, agree on the need for the improvement, limit the budget, and then hire the appropriate designers, contractors and other experts to bring your ideas to reality. If the community can first agree on the need for a new pool to replace the now defunct facility, then Measure UU authorizes up to $19.5 million which will be overseen by a committee and issued based on the final design. Setting a bond limit now and having each household pay for the bond issue is appropriate. I would submit that construction of a beautiful, new, public pool facility in Piedmont in return for a bond issue that costs less than the price of a Starbucks Venti Latte per week, per household, is an affordable and not unreasonable price for Piedmont residents to bear. Please join me in support of Measure UU. We can come together as a community and replace this deteriorated aquatics facility with a new pool facility for future generations to enjoy. Invest in the Commons – Yes on Measure UU By John Ware, AIA In this country and in this city, in particular, there is a significant discrepancy between the amount of money spent on private vs. public improvements. The current situation – crumbling public infrastructure – is the result of years of the community’s inability to fully commit to supporting our public facilities. I see Measure UU to rebuild the Piedmont Community Pool first and foremost as a simple question: whether we, as a community, value a pool or not? City public improvements such as pools, parks, courts, tracks, and trails are the last remaining vestiges of what can be considered the commons – outdoor places that play a central role in both creating community and providing for the simple, nearby enjoyment of the outdoors. In an urban context, we would do well to not let our lives be limited to the experience of individual spaces, such as our cars or our homes. If we let our lives be connected only virtually by digital technologies, we lose out in the richness of experience that our world has to offer. Public financing for a public improvement is appropriate. Does that mean that the City needs to have bids before agreeing on Measure UU? No, it doesn’t. Do you go out and get bids for a bathroom Former East Coast residents say Yes to a new pool By Dave McMurtry Editor: As Piedmont homeowners, our family advocates in favor of Measure UU even though we: 1) have never visited the pool 2) may not use the new pool and 3) are generally opposed to regressive taxes. Why then am I in favor of UU? It’s not because the pool is leaking 3,000 gallons per day and needs to be fixed, or because the increased tax will have a limited impact on our finances at only $30/month (which is well above the average amount for homeowners since we recently purchased our house). Nor is it because I think the initiative is infallibly written. Rather, it is because of the decision we made to live in Piedmont when we relocated from the East Coast four years ago. We seriously considered all of the more affordable surrounding cities, but Piedmont prevailed because of the quality of its schools and, equally as important, its real sense of community. I’ve built my community by taking leadership roles on the boards of the Havens Dads Club and Piedmont Baseball and Softball Foundation, and by coaching the many sports teams that both my elementary school boys are on. So, even though we’re not a “swimming family,” I still believe that Piedmont families who seek community at the pool should have a great facility. Piedmont has invested significantly in the many sports fields and parks that all children and adults in the community enjoy. Those fields are part of the reason that Piedmont is as amazing as it is, and it would be even more so with an updated pool and facility to bring the community together. The ballot initiative isn’t perfect, nor is the timing of raising taxes during a pandemic, but rarely are plans in life perfect. Perfect should not be the enemy of the good. Vote Yes on UU to bring our neighborhoods even closer together at a time when our strong community is more important than ever. The voices of Piedmont’s youth By Julia Stokes, age 10 The existing Piedmont Pool is no longer a decent place to swim. It leaks gallons of heated, chlorinated water a day. It’s simply falling apart. Piedmont can no longer use its pool. But that doesn’t mean it can’t have a pool. I’m way too young to vote, but if I could, I would most definitely vote Yes on Measure UU. If Measure UU doesn’t pass, we will be the only town in all of Alameda County without a pool. Richmond has a pool. Alameda has a pool. Oakland has a pool. We need a pool! What is a community without a pool? We need a pool, especially with the recent heat waves. We have tennis courts. We have playgrounds. We have fields. And we need a pool! The pool was used by a lot of people – the Piedmont Swim Team, water polo teams, lap swimmers, and lots of other people as well. Without a pool, how will kids learn to swim? Piedmont needs a pool. Voting yes on Measure UU is how to get one. Measure UU can fit in City’s Climate Action Plan By Bernard Pech The November 2016 pool study on which Measure UU is based did not take into account the City Climate Action Plan. It called for a pool three times larger than the existing one. I believe that a larger pool could meet the CAB goal if about 150 households committed to installing solar panels on their houses and to assign the energy generated to the City. The current pool energy bill per year is $60,000. At $1.61 per therm it uses 37,267 therms per year. One therm equals 29.3 kWh. Hence 37,267 therms equals 1,091,925 kWh. Let us assume that because of a better design, the proposed pool would need twice rather than three times as much heat energy. One house with 8 panels produces 4,800 kWh. Therefore 454 houses would generate enough electricity to heat the new pool. Given the efficiency factor of three between electric energy and natural gas to generate heat , 454/3 or about 150 houses would be enough (this holds whether the pool uses a natural gas heat exchanger or heat pumps, as natural gas power plants are about 33% efficient to convert natural gas into electricity due to Carnot). The City would be ahead by 37,267 therms per year, thereby also making progress towards the long term 2050 CAB goal. As far as I understand in this forum and others, the proponents of Measure UU have committed to constrain the size of the pool so that it meets the City CAB, and to only issue the proportion of the Measure UU bond adjusted to the pool size compatible with the CAB. Under these conditions, I support Measure UU. I do think that the calculations are correct as the proposed number of houses is certainly in the right order of magnitude. New pool won’t get less expensive with time By Tom and Karen Sullivan Editor: We’re writing in support of Measure UU, which will allow Piedmont to build a new pool facility for the schools and the community. We think a pool is as essential a part of local infrastructure as parks and athletic fields. Our schools should have access to a pool that supports water sports and recreational programs, and community members should have a pool for recreation and exercise. We believe water safety training and basic swimming skills are essential for kids, and swimming is one of the most beneficial forms of exercise for people of all ages. A community pool makes those things possible. The pool is also a hub of F.A.Q. About Piedmont Pool – Measure UU What is Measure UU? Measure UU is a local Bond Measure which will provide funds to construct a safe, sustainable, and affordable community pool for Piedmont families, students, and adults of all ages. Why is Measure UU needed? Built in 1964, the Piedmont Community Pool is well past the end of its useful life and needs to be replaced. Not only are there serious safety issues (on more than one occasion the concrete deck has failed and crumbled into the pool), the locker room facilities are outdated and restrooms do not comply with the Americans with Disability Act (ADA) requirements, the decades-old plumbing is failing and the pool leaks approximately 3,000 gallons of water daily – over a million gallons a year. Without the Piedmont Community Pool, Piedmont would be the only city (and only public school district) in Alameda County without access to a local pool. What will Measure UU funds do? The successful passage of Measure UU ensures that the Piedmont community will continue to have its own local pool facility for school sports/PE programs, lessons, and recreation, for the next 50 years. The cost includes planning, architectural fees, legal fees, demolition and construction for two new pools, restrooms, locker rooms, and community space. The three existing pools will be replaced with two pools to meet resident needs: a warmer recreation pool with areas for safe water play, swim lessons, therapeutic swim, and physical rehabilitation; and a wider and deeper pool for recreation, physical education, water aerobics, water polo, swim team, and lap swimming. How much will Measure UU cost? Measure UU would allow the City to issue up to $19.5M in 30-year fixed rate bonds. Measure UU will cost 2.6 cents per $100 of assessed home value (NOT market rate value). For the median Piedmont home, this works out to less than 75 cents a day. To look up your assessed value, use this link to the Alameda County Assessor’s Office and enter your address: http://acgov. org/MS/prop/index.aspx What happens if Measure UU does not pass? When the 56-year-old Piedmont Pool is permanently closed, there will be no local swimming pool for residents or for Piedmont students. Piedmonters will have to travel and pay to use other communities’ pools, or pay initiation fees and annual dues for private swim clubs. With an empty padlocked pool facility in the center of town, the City will then have to decide what to do with that space. It is important to note that while the City decides, there is a cost to securing the site from blight and vandalism, as well as a significant cost associated with any future use of that space, whether it be for a pool or for some other use. If Measure UU passes, will there be a membership fee to use the pool? No, there is no membership fee. The Piedmont Community Pool has been a public pool since 2011. If Measure UU passes, the municipal bonds will be used to rebuild the pool facility. When the new facility opens, pool users will pay daily use fees, camp and lesson fees, annual and seasonal passes, and facility rentals, to offset operating costs. Pools are different from tennis courts and playing fields (which the City pays to maintain) in that pools are required to have trained staff present on-site during hours of operation (e.g. lifeguards, janitorial services). Like all programs run through the Recreation Department, Piedmont residents will have priority and will pay lower use fees than non-residents. For additional information visit the City of Piedmont’s website and FAQ page: https://piedmont.ca.gov/services___ departments/city_clerk/elections/november_3_2020_general_municipal_election/transfer_tax__pool_bond_measures/ pool_bond_frequently_asked_questions More information is also available at: www.communitypoolforpiedmont.com community life for many; a place where they see friends, meet neighbors, and hold celebrations. The project would include restrooms accessible to users of the adjacent Corey Reich Tennis Center, which currently has no restroom access. This would be a significant improvement to another popular community recreational facility. The pool isn’t the only infrastructure in Piedmont that will need attention in the coming years, and it might be more convenient if we didn’t need to address the pool now. However, it will not get less expensive with time, and, with the extraordinarily low interest rates expected to be in place for the next few years, this is actually the most opportune time to build it. Besides, the state of the current pool is such that it is unlikely to be reopened, as the rates of breakdown, mechanical failures, and leakage have made it no longer feasible to operate. The alternative scenario of a facility chained and closed for an indefinite duration is not, in our opinion, acceptable for a community the caliber of Piedmont. There will likely be more bond measures for other community facilities on the ballot in the coming years. Like all of us, we wish these things were less expensive. But we also think that we have all benefitted from capital investments made by generations past, and we think it is upon us now to make capital See Pool Letters on page 29

articles.text: Piedmont High School principal Adam Littlefield announced recently that the school has hired Bradley Smet of San Luis Obispo as its new Athletic Director Smet, 29, was recently with Templeton High School in San Luis Obispo as their assistant athletic director until stepping in as their interim A.D. He will complete a Master’s Degree in Coaching and Athletic Administration in May. “I’m in the process of moving and looking to stay as close to Piedmont as possible. It’s a beautiful town and I love the area. We have a couple of places on the shortlist now,” said Smet. His experience in managing teams, coaches, and students in the midst of the Coronavirus pandemic undoubtedly played a factor in the hiring process for Piedmont. “I took on the interim (A.D.) role to finish up last year while I was finishing up my Master’s at Concordia University. I was the athletic director (at Templeton) when COVID started, so I got a first-hand look at what was happening, how it affected our kids, and what it meant for high school athletics,” said Smet. The Templeton School District returned to practice ahead of the CIF’s proposed December start for sports, meaning he comes with experience with al school bringing back sports safely and responsibly. “For the lack of a better term, I was fortunate enough to be there at the beginning instead of later on in the process. I know it is different for other counties, but I’ve got to see first-hand how other schools are going about bringing back athletics,” he added. “Everything comes down to what the State (CIF) is allowing, on down to the Alameda County Department of Public Health. We have to manage those two main pieces when putting our plan together,” he said of creating a master sports scheduled for Piedmont High. Smet comes with a background in education as a substitute teacher in the Atascadero Bradley Smet, 29, was hired as Piedmont High’s new Athletic Director. and Templeton Unified School Districts since December 2018; a special education teacher at Atascadero from 2016-2017; and as an elementary school teacher in 2013-2014. A former quarterback for Sterling College in Sterling, Kansas in 2012, Smet began his coaching career as Atascadero High as the JV offensive coordinator from 2013-2015 and in the spring was an assistant varsity baseball coach. He became the baseball team’s JV head coach for 2016. Smet became Atascadero’s varsity football offensive coordinator in 2016 and 2017, and in 2019 he joined Templeton High School’s varsity staff as its quarterbacks and receivers coach. The team finished with a 10-2 record with a league championship, but was upset in the Division 4 Central Coast Quarterfinals as the No. 3 seeded team. His position in Piedmont will be a .6 fulltime equivalent. He takes over after the unexpected departure of Alphonso Powell who spent one year at Piedmont with mixed reviews. Smet will be Piedmont’s fourth athletic director since 2016.

articles.text: With the November ballot looming and Measure UU, the bond that would finance a new pool in Piedmont, we are taking a look at some recent success of the Piedmont High School swim team from 2014-2019. It was led by the Liu sisters, both now swimming for Division 1 Ivy League teams. Skyler Liu, PHS Class of 2017, is at Princeton and younger sister Sasha Liu, Class of 2019, is at Brown U. Starting in 2014, Skyler finished her freshman season at PHS with a record in the Western Alameda County Conference record in the 100 butterfly with a time of 58.09 and went on to improve her time in the North Coast Section trials with a 57.75. The WACC also named her the league’s Swimmer of the Year. She returned to the WACC Finals as a sophomore to drop her 100 fly PR time by over a second to 56.15, then followed up with her first visit to the NCS 100 fly Finals to clock a 55.51, placing 7th of 16. Then as a junior in 2016, Skyler made it a three-peat at the WACC Finals in the 100 butterfly with a 56.40 but also set a league record in the 200 Individual Medley with a time of 2:06.18—her first league title in another event after finishing second in the 200 IM as a freshman and sophomore. She won her second WACC Swimmer of the Year award, earning the honor alongside Bishop O’Dowd’s Catherine Boles Sasha made her first appearance with PHS that year as a freshman as well. She won the WACC’s 500 freestyle in 5:15.02, six seconds ahead of the second-place swimmer. At NCS, Skyler scored some major points for Piedmont in two events. She placed sixth of 16 in the 200 IM with a 2:04.95, then finished fifth of 16 in the 100 Sasha went on to swim for Brown University, and now is in her sophomore year. Staff Photos The Liu sisters helped Piedmont finish 10th out of 43 schools at the North Coast Section swimming championships. Pictured are Sasha Liu (left), Skyler Liu and former PHS coach Victoria Fernandez. fly in 55.20. Her sister, Sasha, reached the NCS Finals in the 500 freestyle, clocking 5:06.18 personal record. Skyler’s senior campaign at the school in 2017 provided her third Swimmer of the Year award after winning every meet she competed in at 200 IM, 100 fly, 100 stroke, and 100 free. She set the WACC’s 200 IM record at 2:05.33, 100 butterfly record at 55.40, and led the relay team to a 2:04.35 victory. As for Sasha, she won her second consecutive WACC 500 freestyle title with a time of 5:04.97 and also set the 100 breaststroke record with a winning time of 1:03.05. Then to North Coast Section, Skyler accounted for 51 of Piedmont’s 81 points. She set her 200 medley record in 2:04.35, finishing fourth of 16. She also placed fifth of 16 in the 100 fly in 56.09. As members of the relay team, the Highlanders won the WACC title and placed eighth of 38 participants in 1:50.08. Though Piedmont only entered six swimmers at NCS, the team finished 10th in a field of 43 schools. Skyler was named our 2017 Piedmont Post Athlete of the Year. Sasha placed second in the 200 IM at North Coast Section, two spots ahead of Skyler, clocking a 2:0281 as a sophomore. Her 2018 junior year would wind up being her final year of competition for Piedmont High after Sasha underwent surgery ahead of her freshman season at Brown. Sasha won her third consecutive WACC 500 freestyle finals by setting the league’s record with a time of 5:02.77 and winning her second consecutive 100 meter breast in 1:03.88. She placed second of 16 in the NCS Finals’ 200 IM with a time of 2:02.63, and also finished fourth in the 100 breast in 1:03.60. Skyler is now entering her senior year at Princeton, prior to the COVID-19 shutdown of sports, she logged times of 27.36 in the 50 freestyle, 33.44 in the 50 breast, 26.76 in the 50 fly, and 1:06.52 in the 100 IM. Sasha competed in seven events as a freshman prior to the shutdown and set a personal record in the 100 breast with a time of 1:03.33, a 2:21.10 in the 200 breast, and a 2:04.37 in the 200 IM. articles.text: Piedmont Park Tennis Courts Piedmont Park Tennis Courts reopened on Monday, October 19, after being resurfaced. The City Council approved an agreement with Vintage Contractors for refurbishment of the Park Tennis Courts in the amount of $97,000. The unanimous approval was made at an August 17 meeting. Recreation Director Chelle Putzer provided an update on the renovations to the Recreation Commission at their October 21 meeting. The city’s four tennis court facilities are resurfaced and repaired on a rotational schedule set by the Facilities Maintenance Plan. Based on condition assessments and discussions with the Recreation Director, the scheduled repair of tennis courts began with Linda Beach Park adjacent to Beach School. Repairs to the Linda Beach courts were completed in 2016. Hampton Park required more substantial repair and was completed in 2017 as part of the comprehensive Hampton Park Improvement Plan. The Recreation Center Tennis Courts was completed in 2019 with overwhelming support from Staff photo the community and is now known as the Corey Reich Tennis Center. The Piedmont Main Park courts were the last to be refurbished. “We are getting rave reviews on how [the courts] play,” Putzer said. The scope of the project in Piedmont Park included resurfacing the two tennis courts with a slipsheet overlay system, similar to the Corey Reich Tennis Center, and the installation of new net posts and nets also, similar to the Corey Reich Tennis Center. All Piedmont tennis courts reopened on May 18 after a twomonth closure due to COVID-19 and shelter-inplace restrictions. Doubles tennis is still not allowed under current state and county regulations. Vice Mayor Teddy Gray King, an avid tennis player, said it is absolutely the right time to move forward in fixing the courts. “Hats off to Sara [Lillevand] for placing this item on the agenda. Everyone loves those courts and [the refurbishment] is the right thing to do with city resources,” King said at the August 17 city council meeting.
articles.title: Park Tennis Courts get a makeover

pages.text: Wednesday, October 28, 2020 13 A look back: Skyler and Sasha Liu’s record setting swim years Park Tennis Courts get a makeover By Jonathan Comeaux With the November ballot looming and Measure UU, the bond that would finance a new pool in Piedmont, we are taking a look at some recent success of the Piedmont High School swim team from 2014-2019. articles.text: 49ers back on track, Raiders look to rebound; Dodgers win World Series; Premier League update The season is at the halfway point of the 2020 season and subsequent trade deadline. The 49ers got back on track against the New England Patriots in a monumental 33-6 win with some the help of four interceptions, and a 112 yard, three touchdown performance by running back Jeffery Wilson. San Francisco faces NFC West leaders, the Seahawks, for a critical matchup this Sunday, November 1, and going to be difficult for the Red and Gold to come out with a win. SF will have to limit Seahawks quarterback Russell Wilson’s productivity and his ability to escapabe on third-downs if thye hope to pull off an upset. They’ll also have to prevent Seattle receiver Tyler Lockett from beating them over the top. Lockett had a monster 15-reception, 200-yard, three-touchdown performance against Arizona. I previously mentioned the 49ers as being possible buyers at the trade deadline for a quarterback, which seems highly unlikely after a two-game winning streak under Jimmy Garoppolo, The 49ers are grasping for cap space with $3 million available this season, so a flashy trade won’t be coming. They have a need for an edge rusher, perhaps a veteran at a discount price would fit. As for the Raiders, they go into Week 8 coming off a 45-20 loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers but are looking ahead to a slightly favorable matchup with the Cleveland Browns. The Browns are a tough team at 5-2 record, but are without WR Odell Beckham Jr. The Silver and Black will be focusing on stopping the league’s No. 1 rushing attack, the Browns’ Nick Chubb and Kareem Hunt. Although Cleveland is favored to win, their bottom ranked pass defense bodes well for Derek Carr and the Raiders’ efficient passing attack. It could come down to which offense is more consistent, something that should favor Vegas. As for the trade deadline, it doesn’t seem likely that Jon Gruden will do much. They are in a bad cap situation next season. Perhaps a defensive lineman with a rookie contract could fit into their scheme. Dodgers win World Series The Dodgers finally got it done, winning the World Series with a 3-1 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 6. A seeming choke-move by the Rays manager was the catalyst for L.A. after Tampa Bay removed starting pitcher Blake Snell in the bottom of the sixth inning when leading 1-0 with a runner on base. It was reminiscent of former Giants manager Dusty Baker removing Russ Ortiz in the 2002 World Series after six and a third innings when up 5-0. Snell was taken after relinquishing his second hit of the game, similar to Ortiz in ‘02. The Dodgers tied the game after a double and wild pitch, then jumped ahead on a fielder’s choice with the speedy Mookie Bets to win this year’s Series. articles.text: Photos courtesy of EBRPD East Bay Regional officially opened the Sutter Regional Shoreline Park at the base of the Bay Bridge and alongside the new bridge segment. East Bay Regional Park District announced on Monday that it will continue its closure of 11 of its parks in the East Bay Hills through today, Wednesday, October 28 due to increased fire activity and safety. “The East Bay Regional Park District is following the NWS issuance of the Red Flag Warnings to be extra cautious, especially in the East Bay hills during these wind events,” said Park District Fire Chief Aileen Theile. “We want to protect people from falling trees or limbs. We apologize for the inconvenience to those who want to access these hill area parks, but the public’s safety is our priority.” Parks that will remain temporarily closed to the public include Wildcat Canyon, Tilden, Reinhardt Redwood, Roberts, Huckleberry, Sibley, Claremont Canyon, Leona Canyon, Anthony Chabot, Lake Chabot and Kennedy Grove. If closures in the East Bay hills continue, these are parks to make note of going forward. The District said that the recent high winds during the weekend caused 14 downed powerlines within or nearby each of the 11 hill area parks. “PGE’s de-energization of these power lines was critical in maintaining safety and not sparking fires from the downed lines. Additional damage to the parks included many fallen trees or tree limbs which park staff are removing to clear roads and trails,” said District spokesman Dave Mason. Mount Diablo State Park experienced winds up to 94 mph at the 1900-foot elevation. Sutter Regional Shoreline Park opens East Bay Regional Park District announced on Wednesday, October 21 that it has opened a new park, Judge John Sutter Regional Shoreline, located at the eastern base of the Bay Bridge. They are calling it the “Gateway to the East Bay” with its visibility to eastbound bridge drivers coming from San Francisco. The new park includes a 600-foot long, 40-foot wide observation deck, built on top the old Bay Bridge. Nearby, East Bay Regional announced the opening of a new event center, the Bridge Yard, which is a renovated 1930s-era electric train maintenance building, now newly minted for concerts, events, and other public concessions. The park also connects with the Bay Bridge Bicycle-Pedestrian Trail that brings hikers and bikers over to Treasure Island. The new park is expected to be a popular tourist destination with sweeping views of the Bay and easy access to Bay Bridge Trail. Judge John Sutter was an East Bay civic and environmental leader and former Park District board member. The new park was part of Sutter’s long-range vision. He saw the potential for a future waterfront park in the 1960s while the area was still active as the Oakland Army Base. He first proposed the park in a 1967 letter to the Association of Bay Area Governments.
articles.title: Judge John Sutter Regional Shoreline Park officially opened

articles.text: More than 6 miles on Hayward Plunge, Greenbelt trails Staff Photos A spillway along Ward Creek on the Hayward Plunge Trail, which is a notoriously haunted park in the East Bay. The trail is popular for mountain bikers with its quick ascents and declines. Eucalyptus trees tower overhead. Travel up the stairs next to Ward Creek to continue on the Hayward Plunge Trail. The hilly trail provides over 1,100 feet in elevation gain over six miles. It’s the week of Halloween, and what better time to delve into all things spooky and haunted? Growing up in the Hayward area, as kids we all heard the gruesome story of the Hayward Plunge Trail at Green Belt Park. The well-known story provided an eerie ghost hunt for teenagers at night. For those easily spooked, be advised that the story isn’t for the faint of heart. Allegedly, a swimming instructor back in the 1960s at the Hayward Plunge indoor pool led his entire class of children up the trail and left them in Ward Creek, telling them to wait until he returned. The children stayed there until the night; the coach returned and murdered them, leaving each of them in the creek. That is the unverified story, which has become a legend. Many locals claim strange sightings, like voices of children around them – sometimes laughter or cries, sounds of footsteps, cold spots, and dark shadows. This writer even had a strange sighting of children all in white garb during the day as a teenager. Spooky stuff, huh? Now that we’re past those horrors, the trail itself is gorgeous. You’ll be hiking under acanopy of California Bay Laurels, Oak trees, and towering Eucalyptus trees. It is known as a premier mountain biking destination in the inner East Bay with its variations of uphill ascents and steep descents. It is considered a technical course, but also possesses a wide, flat surface without any roots or jagged rocks protruding. Starting at Memorial Park, the initial portion of the Hayward Plunge Trail starts in the back of the park past the bandstand. It travels for 1.3 miles slightly uphill alongside Ward Creek until intersecting with Campus Drive and Oaks Drive. Continue up Oaks Drive to the Hayward Plunge Trail. From there, the trail goes for another 1.6 miles to Durham Way and gains 600 feet in elvation through the hills of Green Belt Park. You’ll top out above the tree-line, where you’ll have the option to do a 180 and head back down, or turn right and walk straight down Durham Way to continue the loop onto the Greenbelt Hiking and Riding trail. It reunites you with Ward Creek until reaching Campus Drive. In the six miles of hiking areound noon on a Sunday, we passed only 29 people, so fewer than five people per mile on a popular day for hikers and bikers. The trail is a great spot for a lower leg workout, with over 1,100 feet in elevation gain. No ghost sightings were made, but perhaps my own paranoia brought the feeling that eyes were always following. Punch in “Hayward Plunge” or “Memorial Park Hayward” into your GPS device to access this trail’s parking lot. To cut off the first 1.3 miles, park on Campus Drive.
articles.title: HIKING WITH JON The haunted Hayward Plunge Trail

articles.text: Aurora Theatre Company directors Josh Costello and Dawn Monique Williams are interviewing industry leaders in a series titled “Aurora Connects.” This week, they interviewed Bay Area magician Christian Cagigal. Cagigal is a resident magician at Speakeasy Magick at the McKittrick Hotel in New York City, co-producer for Odd Salon NYC, owner of the San Francisco Ghost Hunt, and co-founder of Fog City Magic Fest. He’s also a five-time winner of the “Best Magician of the Bay” award by the San Francisco Bay Guardian. Costello and Williams will ask Cagigal about his background, how he got started in magic, and what continues to inspire him. Viewers will also learn how the pandemic and shelter-in-place regulations have affected his work, and more about a show that he will be doing at Aurora Theatre in the near future. Cagigal’s previous shows include the popular Pandora Experiment, the long-running OBSCURA, the secretive happenings of The Collection, and the critically acclaimed Now and at the Hour which has been seen in New York, Montréal, Chicago, New Orleans, Minneapolis and San Francisco – Magician Christian Cagigal all shows originally produced by EXIT Theatre. Cagigal can also be seen in the independent, power-pop, musical film, Fruit Fly written and directed by H.P. Mendoza. “Aurora Connects” is Aurora Theatre Company’s weekly live broadcast, which it describes as an “online salon and virtual happy hour.” A broadcast will go live every Friday at 4 p.m. on the company’s YouTube channel. The series is currently in its second season. To view this week’s episode, visit https://www.auroratheatre. org/auroraconnects. articles.text: The Sky’s the Limit – Exhibition Opening Lecture At a time when beauty has never been more important, come be a part of the resilience of the arts. The one element in a painting that can have the greatest impact on the perception of atmosphere is sky. The types of colors used, the cloud composition, the quality of brush stroke....these are some of the details that can effect a viewer’s perception of sky. But this was not always the case. In the world of French classical painting, for instance, the landscape was a mere backdrop for some tale from antiquity or a scene from the Bible. It wasn’t until the late 1700’s that we see greater emphasis on sky: horizon lines dropped as artists began to explore greater variations in the rendering of sky. Indeed, in some art, sky was no longer a backdrop, but rather became the subject. Join artist an art historian Michael Stehr as he presents a zoom lecture to lead us on an examination of sky in painting. This lecture will also serve to open his current exhibition “The Sky’s the Limit!” Michael will also describe his own approach to rendering variable skies.
articles.title: Stehr art exhibit opens Friday at PCA

Aurora Theatre interviews magician Christian Cagigal By Allyson Aleksey Aurora Theatre Company directors Josh Costello and Dawn Monique Williams are interviewing industry leaders in a series titled “Aurora Connects.” This week, they interviewed Bay Area magician Christian Cagigal. Cagigal is a resident magician at Speakeasy Magick at the McKittrick Hotel in New York City, co-producer for Odd Salon NYC, owner of the San Francisco Ghost Hunt, and co-founder of Fog City Magic Fest. He’s also a five-time winner of the “Best Magician of the Bay” award by the San Francisco Bay Guardian. Costello and Williams will ask Cagigal about his background, how he got started in magic, and what continues to inspire him. Viewers will also learn how the pandemic and shelter-in-place regulations have affected his work, and more about a show that he will be doing at Aurora Theatre in the near future. Cagigal’s previous shows include the popular Pandora Experiment, the long-running OBSCURA, the secretive happenings of The Collection, and the critically acclaimed Now and at the Hour which has been seen in New York, Montréal, Chicago, New Orleans, Minneapolis and San Francisco – Magician Christian Cagigal all shows originally produced by EXIT Theatre. Cagigal can also be seen in the independent, power-pop, musical film, Fruit Fly written and directed by H.P. Mendoza. “Aurora Connects” is Aurora Theatre Company’s weekly live broadcast, which it describes as an “online salon and virtual happy hour.” A broadcast will go live every Friday at 4 p.m. on the company’s YouTube channel.
