articles.text: Lafayette-based Gold Coast Chamber Players’ virtual series, Bach Shorts, will end on November 8 with a performance by Robert Howard. Howard, a cellist from American Bach Soloists and Philharmonic Baroque Orchestra, will perform Bach’s Fourth Cello Suite and explore Bach’s universal appeal as he collaborates with cellists from Kenya and Colombia. He will also perform select movements from Bach’s Cello Suites #1, 2, and 3. Bach Connections is the final piece of three performances in the Bach Shorts series. Bach Shorts are one hour, live-streamed performances that seek to connect us through an intimate exploration of The Six Cello Suites by J.S. Bach. The series showcased performances by two prominent Bay Area cellists, Christopher Costanza and Jennifer Kloetzel, and Cellist Robert Howard will conclude next month with Howard. The performance will stream live via YouTube on Sunday, November 8, at 4 p.m. To obtain tickets in advance, visit https:// app.ar ts-people.com /index. php?show=116151.
articles.title: Gold Coast’s Bach Shorts finale on November 8

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony Music Director Joseph Young will celebrate the vibrancy of Berkeley in an evening of music dedicated exclusively to local composers. Berkeley-based composers Samuel Adams, Gabriela Lena Frank, and Myra Melford will join Young in an engrossing program of locally crafted contemporary music. Recently named a Guggenheim Fellow, Adams is a composer of acoustic and electroacoustic music. His work has been hailed as “mesmerizing” and the “music of a composer with a personal voice and keen imagination” by the New York Times, “canny and assured” by the Chicago Tribune, and “wondrously alluring” by the San Francisco Chronicle. He is the son of operatic composer John Adams. Frank, of Lithuanian, Jewish, Peruvian, and Chinese descent, ardently explores her multicultural heritage in her compositions. Her pieces also reflect her studies in Latin American folklore. Jazz pianist Myra Melford. Melford is a pianist and keyboardist with a strong background in Jazz, blues and global folk music. She is also known for her classical, yet avant-garde styles. This week’s episode will air live-stream this Friday, October 30, at 5 p.m. on: https://www. berkeleysymphony.org/josephyoung-friends/. You can also watch the episode later by following the same link. The episode is part of the “Joseph Young and Friends” series presented by Berkeley Symphony, connecting industry leaders in the Bay Area for a virtual discussion on a wide range of topics in classical and contemporary music. The series will conclude on November 19, and will offer a look into the Symphony’s future by showcasing composers Jimmy Lopez and Brian Raphael Nabors.
articles.title: Next episode of Berkeley Symphony’s “Joseph Young and Friends” airs this Friday

articles.text: Michael Tilson Thomas meets his idol, James Brown, in a new documentary made available through PBS. Michael Tilson Thomas: Where Now Is, a full-length documentary exploring the life and career of the renowned conductor, premiered on October 23 is now available to stream. It is part of the American Masters series. The documentary follows Michael Tilson Thomas from his childhood in California to the world stage and his leadership roles with the San Francisco Symphony and New World Symphony. The film features original interviews with Tilson Thomas and other classical music luminaries, including composer Steve Reich, Los Angeles Philharmonic CEO Chad Smith, pianist Ralph Grierson, Boston Symphony Orchestra CEO Mark Volpe, San Francisco Chronicle music critic Joshua Kosman, and many more. The film incorporates concert footage from Tilson Thomas’ youth through the present, performing with the San Francisco, New World, Boston and London Symphonies. In addition, Where Now Is also showcases a conversation between Tilson Thomas and his idol, legendary rhythm and blues vocalist James Brown, whose song “Cold Sweat” inspired Tilson Thomas’ concept of timing. The documentary is made available through PBS as part of its American Masters series. It can be viewed through the PBS video application, or pbs.org/ americanmasters. Visit https:// www.pbs.org/wnet/americanmasters/michael-tilson-thomas-documentary/15245/ for more information. articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet has announced its 2021 repertory season, to run from January 19 to June 27, 2021. The seven-program season features four world premieres and one West Coast premiere over the first three programs between January 19 and February 22, followed by Balanchine’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream to run from March 5 through March 31, and Jewels to run from March 25 through March 31. The 2021 repertory season will conclude with ballet artistic director Helgi Tomasson’s Swan Lake, May 28 through June 6, and Romeo and Juliet from June 18 through June 27. Commissions include works by Bay Area choreographer Danielle Rowe, San Francisco Ballet soloist Myles Thatcher, and Mark Morris, as well as two new works previously scheduled for the 2020 San Francisco Ballet’s 2021 repertory season will conclude with Romeo and Juliet. Season: Mrs. Robinson by Cathy Marston and American Ballet Theatre co-commission The Seasons by Alexei Ratmansky. San Francisco Ballet will be observing strict adherence to state and local health protocols, and the program as announced remains flexible and subject to change. For tickets and more information visit www.sfballet.org.
articles.title: SF Ballet announces 2021 repertory season

articles.text: Celebrate Halloween with Cal Performances by watching a special, live-stream of Manual Cinema’s Frankenstein. For Cal Performances’ “Cal at Home” series, Manual Cinema has created a new iteration of its acclaimed Frankenstein production, made specifically for home viewing. The performance will premiere tomorrow, Thursday, October 29, at 7 p.m., and will be available on demand through January 27, 2021. The production, which was co-commissioned by Cal Performances, weaves together the plot of Mary Shelley’s gothic tale with themes of desire, birth, and loss from the author’s own biography – asking us to consider our responsibility to our modern-day creations. The company’s performers manipulate hundreds of paper puppets to create a silent animated film in real time, featuring live actors and an immersive score performed onstage by four Sarah Fornance in Manual Cinema’s Frankenstein. musicians. The production was devised by Drew Dir, Sarah Fornance, and Julia Miller, with puppet design by Dir and Lizi Breit, and original music and sound design by Ben Kauffman and Kyle Vegter. Court Theatre presented the world premiere of Frankenstein in Chicago in late 2018, and Frankenstein has its New York premiere at the Public Theatre’s Under the Radar Festival in January 2019. Its international debut occurred at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival in Scotland in August 2019. To watch tomorrow’s stream, visit https://calperformances.org/ events/2020-21/theater/manual-cinema-frankenstein/#cal-performances-suggested-pricing.
articles.title: Cal Performances hosts Frankenstein, streaming tomorrow

articles.text: World famous boxer Joe Louis pursued a career in boxing rather than as a violinist. Joseph Louis Barrow. You probably don’t recognize the name, even though he was very famous. He was the grandson of slaves, born in Alabama. The family moved to Detroit to get away from the violent racism. Times were tough in the Great Depression. To make matters even worse, Joseph’s father was abusive. He deserted the family and died in a mental institution. Joseph’s mother was gentle and loving, and she wanted her son to become a violinist. She knew about other violinists of African descent. France had the flamboyant Chevalier de St-George, and in England there was a composer, Samuel Coleridge-Taylor. In Vienna there was Beethoven’s friend, George Bridgetower. It was for Bridgetower that Beethoven wrote his brilliant “Kreutzer sonata”. They all had African parents. America had Clarence Cameron White and William Grant Still. I knew maestro Still. But back to Barrow. Mrs. Barrow envisioned greatness for her son. She believed he would be world famous. He was but in a different art far removed from the violin. Joseph did have an aptitude for the violin, but, as I said, times were tough. A career in music was especially hard. Orchestras were out of work and musicians often played in restaurants and in cafeterias. Joseph wanted a better life for himself and for his family, but he had no education. While he loved the violin, he was forced to make other plans. He was big and strong, but football and baseball were segregated. That left only boxing. So, it was boxing that was his passport to fame and fortune. (I use the last word for effect only. The IRS treated Joseph horribly.) Joseph became a success as a boxer. Joseph never used his last name professionally, and he shortened his first name to Joe. And thus, the aspiring violinist Joseph Louis Barrow became boxing legend Joe Louis. Next week: The story of two violinists who changed history.
articles.title: Fame and success

articles.text: The Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive hosted an “artist talk” with New Delhi-based photographer Gauri Gill. In this recorded talk in conjunction with the exhibition When All That Is Solid Melts into Air, Gill addresses her practice and how it has evolved over the recent past, as well as its formative roots. She speaks about various collaborative projects, including Fields of Sight –represented in the exhibition by the work A Seed’s Journey (2019) – and her ongoing engagement with the so-called “other,” including her work in rural India since 1999. Gill’s projects highlight her belief in collaboration and in using photography as a memory Photographer Gauri Gill practice. Her work addresses the twinned Indian identity marks of caste, class, and community as determinants of mobility and social behavior; it is marked by empathy, surprise, and concern over issues of survival. Visit https://bampfa.org/event/ artists-talk-gauri-gill to watch the discussion.
articles.title: Berkeley Art Museum hosts Artist Talk with photographer Gauri Gill

articles.text: As of Friday, October 23, restaurants were given the green light by the Alameda County Public Health Department to reopen for indoor dining, subject to 25 percent capacity or 100 people, whichever is fewer. Indoor dining was not allowed as of March 17 due to the coronavirus epidemic. Many restaurants adapted by creating outdoor dining spaces, which eventually became permissible by the county. It hasn’t been a seamless transition; in July the County suspended outdoor dining because it had not obtained variance from the state, causing confusion for restaurant owners who already moved outdoors. Despite the recent approval for indoor dining by the county, many restaurants are opting to remain outdoors for the time being. There is a similar trend in San Francisco, where indoor dining was permitted on September 30, but many are choosing to keep their tables outdoors. On October 13, the state an nou nced that Alameda County entered the less-restrictive orange tier, allowing for some business sectors to begin reopening. COVID-19 case rates, testing positivity and hospitalizations are stable, allowing Alameda County to continue moving at a measured pace to open or expand activities permitted under the Red Tier and some activities that are permitted under the orange tier. “Case rates are rising across the country and we continue to monitor the impact of activities that were previously permitted locally. With flu season nearly here, we must be vigilant and not move so quickly as to initiate a surge in cases that could result in hospitalizations and deaths,” Alameda County Public Health Officer Neetu Balram said. She added that Alameda County moves at a more measured pace than the State in order to avoid a sharp rise in cases. “It’s important for every resident to consider the potential risk of getting or spreading COVID- 19 and how they can participate in these newly opened activities safely,” said Dr. Nicholas Moss, Alameda County Interim Health Officer. “Outdoor activities with fewer people are safer. It is increasingly less safe if more people are in attendance, if the activities are indoors, or if people are frequently removing their face coverings.”
articles.title: Restaurants in county OK’d for indoor dining

articles.text: Piedmont COVID-19 caseload increases to 43 Alameda County updated its shelter in place order on Friday, October 23 and the rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in the county is currently 1.4 percent. This positivity rate has stayed below 2 percent throughout October. The new health orders reflect the county’s position as an Orange Tier county, the second-least restrictive tier for reopening the economy, according to state metrics. The state placed Alameda County into the Orange Tier (Moderate Tier) on October 13, although county officials have said it would take time to determine how to reopen. Indoor dining is now allowed according to the revised order, but capacity must be restricted to 25 percent or 100 people, whichever is fewer. Some indoor family entertainment centers, like bowling alleys and climbing walls, can reopen, as well as indoor worship services, movie theaters and gyms, all with capacity restrictions. Capacity restrictions for indoor retail and malls have been increased to 50 percent. “It’s important for every resident to consider the potential risk of getting or spreading COVID-19 and how they can participate in these newly opened activities safely,” Dr. Nicholas Moss, Alameda County Interim Health Officer, said in a statement. “Outdoor activities with fewer people are safer. It is increasingly less safe if more people are in attendance, if the activities are indoors, or if people are frequently removing their face coverings.” Two new cases of COVID- 19 were recorded in Piedmont in the past week, according to Alameda County Health Public Health Department data released yesterday, Tuesday, October 27. In total, 43 cases have been reported in the City since the coronavirus pandemic began in March. Overall, the caseload in Alameda County is 23,471, an increase of over 650 cases from one week ago. The county has recorded 462 total COVID-19 fatalities. In Oakland, the most populous city in Alameda County, the number of cases has now reached 9,064. In Hayward, 3,475 cases have been recorded and there have been 1,633 reported in Fremont. San Leandro has reported 1,291 and Livermore reported 1,004. More Bay Area counties moved into the Orange Tier, the second-least restrictive tier out of four according to California’s color-coded system, this week. Marin, Contra Costa, Santa Clara and San Mateo counties are all in the Orange Tier. San Francisco was moved into the Yellow Tier, the least restrictive “Minimal” tier, last week. Alameda County is close to meeting benchmarks for the Yellow Tier, except that the county’s cases per day per 100,000 remains too high. The county is counting 3.2 cases per 100,000 people, while a county must have 1 case per 100,000 or fewer to be in the Yellow Tier. As of press time, 904,198 cases of COVID-19 have been recorded in California. There have been 17,400 deaths due to the disease statewide. While California had the most cases in the United States for several months, Texas now has a higher caseload of 916,562, according to New York Times analysis. Gov. Gavin Newsom said Monday, October 26 that the state will independently review vaccines approved by the Food and Drug Administration before distribution can occur in California. One day later, western states Washington, Oregon and Nevada announced they would join California’s vaccine review group. “This vaccine plan will move at the speed of trust,” Newsom said in a press conference this week. “You have to have confidence in the efficacy of the vaccine, confidence that we’re not rushing to judgement in terms of its distribution and its accessibility.” The City of Piedmont last week echoed guidance from the county noting that trick-or-treating on Saturday, Halloween, is considered a high-risk activity and is not recommended. articles.text: Biologist Audra Barrios brings a live reptile and amphibian demonstration to the San Francisco Conservatory of Flowers. The San Francisco Conservatory of Flowers will host a “creepy, crawly” live animal demo this Friday, October 30, just in time for Halloween. The class will take place over teleconference application Zoom, between 6 p.m. and 7 p.m. Audra Barrios, Executive Director of Things That Creep, will introduce viewers to herpetology, the study of reptiles and amphibians. Barrios is a biologist and educator in the San Francisco Bay Area for over 12 years. Through her travels to Madagascar and Mexico, she saw a need for a conservation organization focused on underrepresented critters such as reptiles and amphibians. During the class, you will meet three unique species of geckos, including the Caledonian Giant Gecko, the largest gecko in the world. This event is recommended for children but is suitable for all ages. Class will include a virtual tour and scavenger hunt. General admission tickets are $18. There is also an option to purchase a $30 admission ticket, which includes a “Conservatory at Home” kit. The kit will include an “Air Plant,” hands-on activities, a hand lens, and a Conservatory pin. pages.text: Wednesday, October 28, 2020 19 News Restaurants in county OK’d for indoor dining By Allyson Aleksey As of Friday, October 23, restaurants were given the green light by the Alameda County Public Health Department to reopen for indoor dining, subject to 25 percent capacity or 100 people, whichever is fewer. Indoor dining was not allowed as of March 17 due to the coronavirus epidemic. Many restaurants adapted by creating outdoor dining spaces, which eventually became permissible by the county. It hasn’t been a seamless transition; in July the County suspended outdoor dining because it had not obtained variance from the state, causing confusion for restaurant owners who already moved outdoors. Despite the recent approval for indoor dining by the county, many restaurants are opting to remain outdoors for the time being. There is a similar trend in San Francisco, where indoor dining was permitted on September 30, but many are choosing to keep their tables outdoors. On October 13, the state an nou nced that Alameda County entered the less-restrictive orange tier, allowing for some business sectors to begin reopening. COVID-19 case rates, testing positivity and hospitalizations are stable, allowing Alameda County to continue moving at a measured pace to open or expand activities permitted under the Red Tier and some activities that are permitted under the orange tier. “Case rates are rising across the country and we continue to monitor the impact of activities that were previously permitted locally. With flu season nearly here, we must be vigilant and not move so quickly as to initiate a surge in cases that could result in hospitalizations and deaths,” Alameda County Public Health Officer Neetu Balram said. She added that Alameda County moves at a more measured pace than the State in order to avoid a sharp rise in cases. “It’s important for every resident to consider the potential risk of getting or spreading COVID- 19 and how they can participate in these newly opened activities safely,” said Dr. Nicholas Moss, Alameda County Interim Health Officer. “Outdoor activities with fewer people are safer. It is increasingly less safe if more people are in attendance, if the activities are indoors, or if people are frequently removing their face coverings.” SF Conservatory of Flowers hosts animal event October 30 event features amphibians, reptiles Alameda County revises health orders to reflect Orange Tier status Piedmont COVID-19 caseload increases to 43 By Barry Eitel Alameda County updated its shelter in place order on Friday, October 23 and the rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in the county is currently 1.4 percent. This positivity rate has stayed below 2 percent throughout October. The new health orders reflect the county’s position as an Orange Tier county, the second-least restrictive tier for reopening the economy, according to state metrics. The state placed Alameda County into the Orange Tier (Moderate Tier) on October 13, although county officials have said it would take time to determine how to reopen. Indoor dining is now allowed according to the revised order, but capacity must be restricted to 25 percent or 100 people, whichever is fewer. Some indoor family entertainment centers, like bowling alleys and climbing walls, can reopen, as well as indoor worship services, movie theaters and gyms, all with capacity restrictions. Capacity restrictions for indoor retail and malls have been increased to 50 percent. “It’s important for every resident to consider the potential risk of getting or spreading COVID-19 and how they can participate in these newly opened activities safely,” Dr. Nicholas Moss, Alameda County Interim Health Officer, said in a statement. “Outdoor activities with fewer people are safer. It is increasingly less safe if more people are in attendance, if the activities are indoors, or if people are frequently removing their face coverings.” Two new cases of COVID- 19 were recorded in Piedmont in the past week, according to Alameda County Health Public Health Department data released yesterday, Tuesday, October 27. In total, 43 cases have been reported in the City since the coronavirus pandemic began in March. Overall, the caseload in Alameda County is 23,471, an increase of over 650 cases from one week ago. The county has recorded 462 total COVID-19 fatalities. In Oakland, the most populous city in Alameda County, the number of cases has now reached 9,064. In Hayward, 3,475 cases have been recorded and there have been 1,633 reported in Fremont. San Leandro has reported 1,291 and Livermore reported 1,004. More Bay Area counties moved into the Orange Tier, the second-least restrictive tier out of four according to California’s color-coded system, this week. Marin, Contra Costa, Santa Clara and San Mateo counties are all in the Orange Tier. San Francisco was moved into the Yellow Tier, the least restrictive “Minimal” tier, last week. Alameda County is close to meeting benchmarks for the Yellow Tier, except that the county’s cases per day per 100,000 remains too high. The county is counting 3.2 cases per 100,000 people, while a county must have 1 case per 100,000 or fewer to be in the Yellow Tier. As of press time, 904,198 cases of COVID-19 have been recorded in California. There have been 17,400 deaths due to the disease statewide. While California had the most cases in the United States for several months, Texas now has a higher caseload of 916,562, according to New York Times analysis. Gov. Gavin Newsom said Monday, October 26 that the state will independently review vaccines approved by the Food and Drug Administration before distribution can occur in California. One day later, western states Washington, Oregon and Nevada announced they would join California’s vaccine review group. “This vaccine plan will move at the speed of trust,” Newsom said in a press conference this week. “You have to have confidence in the efficacy of the vaccine, confidence that we’re not rushing to judgement in terms of its distribution and its accessibility.” The City of Piedmont last week echoed guidance from the county noting that trick-or-treating on Saturday, Halloween, is considered a high-risk activity and is not recommended. articles.text: The Piedmont Council of the Boy Scouts of America (BSA) has announced the retirement of Executive Director Jo Hazelett, after 22 years of service in the position. Hazelett will officially end her two-decade long tenure on Saturday, October 31 (also known as Halloween). Hazlett began her career with the Piedmont Scout Council in November 1998. Before coming to Piedmont, she worked with the American Red Cross as a Disaster Services Director in Phoenix, Arizona for approximately 3 years. Before she joined the Piedmont BSA, she worked with the East Bay Conservation Corps, now known as the Civicorps Schools. The Civicorps Academy serves young adults ages 18 to 26 through a combination of on-thejob training in environmental improvement projects. “Through these experiences I became interested in how nonprofits sustain themselves,” she said. “Nonprofits needed money to survive; without money, there would be no program.” Hazelett came to the position in an unusual way, explained Dale Radcliff, a former Piedmont Council president and now Western Region BSA Vice President. “Twenty-two years ago, Wes Smith, Bob Lambing Sr. and I were designated a subcommittee of the Piedmont Council board to find a new Executive Director. At the time, our small Boy Scout council was not allowed to have a conforming Scout Executive and our subcommittee was forced to look for candidates outside the professional Scouting community. To our good fortune we and Jo Hazelett found each other and the rest is history,” Radcliff said. Hazelett recalled that she applied for the position because she was interested in running an organization after years of experience in development in the nonprofit sector. She noted that at the time of her hiring there were very few female directors in the Boy Scouts organization. “I may have been the second or third [female director] in the country,” she explained. Under Hazelett’s leadership, the Piedmont Council has been ranked first among the nation’s 253 councils on the Journey to Excellence (JTE) metric for the last four years. It is also the BSA. At the time, Boy Scouts of America spokesman Gregg Shields said if the Piedmont Council flouted the ban, it would be the first council in the country to do so. “All of a sudden it became a national story,” Hazelett said. “We just said that we didn’t find anything in the oath and law that would appear to sanction discrimination of any kind.” The ban on openly gay scouts was eventually lifted in 2013, in part with the leadership for 10 years of a few Piedmont Scout leaders. Piedmont’s inclusive council proved to be seminal. The addition of girls to the Piedmont Boy Scouts, which came about recently, was another milestone that Hazelett said was “a long time coming” in the world of scouting. “Over the years, not only did Jo work collaboratively with 11 separate board presidents, but during that time presided over our Piedmont Council regaining conforming council status, witnessing Scouting become more diverse and inclusive (Piedmont was at the forefront of national membership policy change) and the addition of girls to our traditionally all-male programs,” Radcliff said. The Piedmont Boy Scouts experienced another significant milestone under Hazelett’s tutelage. Piedmont entered the debate over the national organization’s anti-gay stance, with a letter to scout parents and the scouting community saying that the Piedmont Scout did not discriminate. Hazelett explained that the conversation began early in her time in Piedmont, in 2000. At a board retreat, council members decided that they did not think being gay violated scouting principles. “As a council, we really had no choice but to follow the rules [of the national council]. Someone had the brilliant idea to pull out the Scout Oath and Law, and each person on the board took a piece and read,” Hazelett said. “When we got through the whole thing, we sort of sat and looked at each other, and it was pretty obvious what we needed to do.” A “carefully-crafted letter” was then sent to the Piedmont community expressing their findings, which then came to the attention of the national offices of Jo with Mr. Cody on the ridge smallest council in the U.S. Bob Coleman, a past president of the Piedmont council, praised Hazelett for her achievements as Executive Director. “The Piedmont Boy Scout Council has been particularly fortunate to have enjoyed the leadership of Jo Hazelett. Under her leadership as Scout Executive Piedmont has earned the highest national BSA Journey to Excellence scores in the nation,” he said. “The JTE score sheet measures a council across a broad range of criteria, but is particularly focused on the depth and quality of the scouting program offered as well as the financial well-being of the council. The measures that are counted are the number of eagle scout ranks earned. “Piedmont rates as the smallest council in the country, yet it easily leads the nation in the percentage of youth participating in the community. Piedmonts numbers always seem to exceed 60 percent, where the national norm is 6 percent. Also, the council’s per capita endowment is far and away the strongest in the nation,” Coleman added. Hazelett said that bringing financial security to the Piedmont Council BSA is one of her greatest achievements during her tenure. When she started in 1998, the council’s endowment fund was approximately $300,000. She will be leaving the council with a $7 million endowment this year, one of the highest endowments in BSA history. The Council credits Coleman with raising much of that money. “It became very clear to me, very quickly, that money was the thing that was going to keep the organization going, as with any organization. But that was the message I kept telling the Board [of Directors], and Bob Coleman understood that and worked hard to get us to where we needed to be,” she said. Her efforts have also been aided, in large part, by the Bechtel Foundation. The Bechtel family, originally from Piedmont, and its Foundation created the Summit Bechtel Family National Scout Reserve in West Virginia with a $50 million donation to the National Boy Scouts of America. The land, encompassing 14,000 acres, is now the site of the National Jamboree each summer. “One memory that stands out,“ recounted Hazelett, “was in 2010 when Stephen Bechtel, Jr., a Piedmont Eagle Scout from Troop 4, learned that I had never been to a [National] Jamboree. He insisted on picking up my husband, my dog, and me as we ended a section hike on the Continental Divide in Montana and taking us to the Jamboree in West Virginia on his jet,” she said with a smile. “We had a blast. It sort of ruined commercial flying for us for a while!” “I believe that without Jo’s Jo on latrine detail at the BSA Scouting Jamboree Jo leading a Piedmont Scouting celebration

articles.text: Election Day is little more than a week away. As a citizen, you may feel the results will affect many aspects of life in this country. But as an investor, your situation probably won’t change after the votes are counted. No matter who wins, the financial markets may well show some politically driven volatility, but that often happens around elections, and it typically doesn’t last long. But what about the longer term? How might changes in policy and new legislation affect your investment outlook? To begin, keep in mind that many campaign promises remain just that – promises. And even when some of them are enacted, any ultimate legislation may be quite different from what was proposed on the campaign trail. Still, sometime in the future, we could see election-related changes that could affect your investment strategy. For example, over the years, we’ve seen many adjustments in the tax rates of capital gains and stock dividends, and it’s likely these rates will change again one day. When that happens, you may need to look at the equities portion of your portfolio to see if you want to make some adjustments. Many other changes, though, are hard to predict. It’s possible that future legislation could affect specific industries, either positively or negatively. Such moves could also influence the way you look at certain investments, but if you have a diversified portfolio that contains a broad mix of stocks, bonds and other securities, any actions affecting one particular industry probably won’t cause you to significantly adjust holdings invested in other sectors. In any case, while it may be a good idea to keep an eye open for things like tax rate changes or how new policies may affect different market segments, your main emphasis, in terms of your investment decisions, should remain on your goals and what you need to do to achieve them. At least once each year, review your portfolio carefully to make sure your investments are aligned with your goals, whether they are short-term (a new car, a long vacation and so on) or long-term (such as college for your children or a comfortable retirement). Periodically, depending on what’s happening in your life and the progress of your investment portfolio, you may need to evaluate your goals to ensure they’re prioritized appropriately to help keep you on track toward achieving what’s most important to you. Over time, your goals may change, too. Perhaps you’ve decided that instead of retiring early and traveling around the world, you now want to turn your hobby into a business. Changing this goal may require a different investment strategy. Or you might change your mind about where you want to live – instead of staying in your home, as originally planned, you might downsize and move to a different area. Your goals may change in many ways, all of which may warrant updating your investment strategies. Here’s the key point: You’re the one electing to make these changes. No matter what happens in this or any other election, be sure to “vote” for the strategies that have the potential for a winning outcome. articles.text: a Bernese Mountain Dog Dear Abby: To celebrate a “Socially- Distanced” Halloween and to say thank you to all our Piedmont clients, Ryan and I and one of our dog walkers, are going to take our regular dog-walking clients for a Halloween dress-up walk in Piedmont on October 30th at Dracena Park. It’s a fun way to get the dogs out and take super cute “Howl-O-Weener” photos of our clients. We have been doing this for about five years now. We get the dogs dressed amd get to Dracena about 9:30 a.m. We start our walk by the little area where the kids play, keeping a distance, then making our way up the bridge and over to the large lawn area up top. We have Hazel, Maya, Alfie, Kayley, Josie, Bogie, Bugsy, Maggie, Violet, Harvey, Agnes, Leo & Beau all dressing up. We are not out all that long, maybe an hour. We will try to be at the bottom of Dracena around 9:30 a.m., but it depends on how many people stop us to take pictures or pet the dogs. Our clients love getting a picture of their dogs dressed up as a princess or an avocado or super dog. So dress up and join us or just come in your dog coats! We will be wearing shaggy masks. -Heidi, Owner of Pawsitively Pampered Pets Your October 30th walk works out well because I wasn’t sure about organizing a Piedmont Halloween dog party this year (usually at 8:30 a.m. by Bushy Del Creek on Halloween morning, October 31st). pages.text: 22 Wednesday, October 28, 2020 Features Dear Abby A pet column compiled by Piedmont pets Voting for a solid investment strategy By T.J. Stevko Election Day is little more than a week away. As a citizen, you may feel the results will affect many aspects of life in this country. But as an investor, your situation probably won’t change after the votes are counted. No matter who wins, the financial markets may well show some politically driven volatility, but that often happens around elections, and it typically doesn’t last long. But what about the longer term? How might changes in policy and new legislation affect your investment outlook? To begin, keep in mind that many campaign promises remain just that – promises. And even when some of them are enacted, any ultimate legislation may be quite different from what was proposed on the campaign trail. Still, sometime in the future, we could see election-related changes that could affect your investment strategy. For example, over the years, we’ve seen many adjustments in the tax rates of capital gains and stock dividends, and it’s likely these rates will change again one day. When that happens, you may need to look at the equities portion of your portfolio to see if you want to make some adjustments. Many other changes, though, are hard to predict. It’s possible that future legislation could affect specific industries, either positively or negatively. Such moves could also influence the way you look at certain investments, but if you have a diversified portfolio that contains a broad mix of stocks, bonds and other securities, any actions affecting one particular industry probably won’t cause you to significantly adjust holdings invested in other sectors. In any case, while it may be a good idea to keep an eye open for things like tax rate changes or how new policies may affect different market segments, your main emphasis, in terms of your investment decisions, should remain on your goals and what you need to do to achieve them. At least once each year, review your portfolio carefully to make sure your investments are aligned with your goals, whether they are short-term (a new car, a long vacation and so on) or long-term (such as college for your children or a comfortable retirement). Periodically, depending on what’s happening in your life and the progress of your investment portfolio, you may need to evaluate your goals to ensure they’re prioritized appropriately to help keep you on track toward achieving what’s most important to you. Over time, your goals may change, too. Perhaps you’ve decided that instead of retiring early and traveling around the world, you now want to turn your hobby into a business. Changing this goal may require a different investment strategy. Or you might change your mind about where you want to live – instead of staying in your home, as originally planned, you might downsize and move to a different area. Your goals may change in many ways, all of which may warrant updating your investment strategies. Here’s the key point: You’re the one electing to make these changes. No matter what happens in this or any other election, be sure to “vote” for the strategies that have the potential for a winning outcome. articles.text: Jeanie Menke, the mother of Mark Menke of Piedmont, passed away on October 4, 2020 in Austin, Texas after a courageous 16-year battle with Parkinson’s Disease. She was 89. Born Jeanie Fay Rosenbaum on January 14, 1931 in rural Calhoun County, Texas, she was the daughter of Melvin Rosenbaum, Sr. and Alma Jaster Rosenbaum. Jeanie was a warm and loving wife, mother, grandmother and friend who faced Parkinson’s with grace, and did not let the disease keep her from living a rich and varied life. Under a soft exterior, Jeanie was intelligent and determined, qualities appreciated by those who knew her. Her faith was a strength and comfort to her always. She grew up on a farm outside of Port Lavaca, Texas, where she was Port Lavaca High School Valedictorian in 1948. After attending Southwestern Business School in Houston, Jeanie returned to Port Lavaca and became one of the early employees at Alcoa’s Point Comfort Works, where she worked as a secretary starting in 1950. At Point Comfort Works, Jeanie met Allen Menke of Victoria, Texas, and the two were married in 1952. The Menkes transferred to Rockdale, Texas with the 1952 opening of the Rockdale Alcoa plant. There, Allen began a 37-year career as a human resources manager, while Jeanie worked as a secretary until the birth of their first child in 1954. Jeanie and Allen had four children: Mark, James, Mary and Laura. She raised four successful children and nurtured a strong family culture that continues to this day. As her children married, Jeanie embraced her children’s spouses and became a loving grandmother and great grandmother to successive generations. Together, theme including live music and dancing. After Allen passed away in 1995, Jeanie held down the family farm until her Parkinson’s Disease required her to move into assisted living in 2014. She lived her last five years in Brookdale Northwest Hills in Austin. There she made friends with other residents and staff and was always looking for a bridge game. She even kept up her secretarial skills, using her computer to follow friends and family on email and Facebook. The family thanks the staff at Brookdale Northwest Hills for their many years of loving care. Jeanie is survived by son, Mark Menke and wife, Anne-Marie Lamarche of Piedmont, California, and their children Elise (Evan Stuller), Claire (Daniel Priestley) and Alexander, and a great granddaughter Emilie-Marie Faye Stuller; by son James Menke and wife, Beth of Austin, Texas and their four children Andrew (Nicole), Bryan (Rachel), Audrey, and Joseph (Emma) and two great grandsons Cameron and Lucas Menke (Andrew); by daughter Mary Strickland and husband Gary of Coleman, Texas and their two children Matt and Erin (Isla Cameron); and daughter Laura Arroyo and husband, Charles of Round Rock, Texas, and their three sons Brandon (Maureen Naval), Wesley (Natalie) and Connor. She is predeceased by her husband, Allen Menke, and brother Melvin Rosenbaum. A memorial service will be held at Peace Lutheran Church in Rockdale, Texas, on November 28 at 11 a.m. In lieu of flowers, the family requests that memorial donations be made to Peace Lutheran Church, P. O. Box 308, Rockdale, TX 76567 or The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research (www.michaeljfox.org). Jeanie Menke, the mother of Piedmont resident Mark Menke, died on October 4 in Austin, Texas. She was 89. Jeanie and Allen invested countless hours of labor and love to build their Rockdale farm, home and gardens from native Texas woodlands. The farm has become a living legacy and family gathering space for their children and grandchildren. Jeanie was an active member of Peace Lutheran Church in Rockdale for over 60 years, serving as church secretary for 23 years, assisting Pastors Waldemar Wendell and Herbert Lammert. She was an avid bridge player and a member of several bridge groups, including a couples’ bridge group with her husband. Jeanie had a closeknit group of friends in Rockdale who loved taking day trips around Central Texas, as well as extended travel and cruises around the U.S. Jeanie also traveled regularly to California to visit her son and his family, and to Europe to visit grandchildren who were studying abroad. Recognizing her love of travel, Jeanie’s 80th birthday was celebrated with an “Around the World in 80 Days” WE PROVIDE: • Excellent in-home care • Quality caregiver training • Errands and transportation Start home care today. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. articles.text: Editor: Our home values are linked to Piedmont’s historical reputation for excellent schools. That reputation is starting to falter as evidenced by the unexpected loss of 81 students from our school district this year. Once lost, it will take years to recover our reputation. Hari Titan is the School Board candidate who will add thoughtful management and responsible oversight to the School Board. Since 2013 he’s contributed over 500 hours of time which produced well-conceived recommendations that saved our schools and taxpayers millions of dollars. Our current school board is disproportionately influenced by the unions and our country-club society. Board decisions are too often unanimous with little public deliberation and are often dismissive of thoughtful public input. Titan will return transparent governance to the school board. My decision to vote for Hari is based on the content of his character and intellect. His experience as a businessman, mathematician, scientist, and STEM college professor brings valuable diversity and professional acumen to the board. Membership on the school board should not be a popularity contest. Titan is the responsible candidate we need.
articles.title: Titan: 7 years of valuable aid to schools

articles.text: Donald Chandler AIA Comprehensive immigration reform. Comprehensive Covid relief. Goals to which to aspire. Doesn’t Piedmont deserve a comprehensive solution to our known physical planning issues and a financial response to those issues? Those issues include (but are not limited to): • Our Essential Services Buildings – Fire and Police Buildings and City Hall; • Our Recreational facilities including the Community Pool; • The State Mandated Affordable Housing requirement. ( possibly several hundred units) We need a Land Use Plan and a Comprehensive Financing Plan for all these projects. How can we be asked to vote for only one project, the Community Pool, without a comprehensive plan? A No vote on UU gives the City a ‘break in the action’ and the time to address the investigations, planning, estimates required to present credible financing options to the voters -- and also time to implement a Plan B – a repair/ rehab of the pool at a cost of $3-5 million that could take as little as 6 months to complete. Plan B for the Community Pool has already been outlined in a study completed for the City Council in 2018. There has been a lot of rhetoric about Measure UU. Let’s look at some direct quotes from the Alameda County Voter Guide. 1. “Therefore, the City Council cannot guarantee that the bonds will provide sufficient funds to allow completion of all the needed improvements.” Is this prudent fiscal planning? Would you start a project on your home if you didn’t have sufficient funds? We say No. 2. “If Measure UU does not pass, the Piedmont Community Pool is on track to be closed permanently.” Is this proper civic behavior or just a scare tactic? Any prudent City action must have a backup plan and not just state that residents will be faced with “an empty padlocked pool”. 3. “The pool leaks approximately 3000 gallons of water a day.” The City has a study that states the leak can be repaired for $ 50-60,000 (while the leak costs the City over $10,000 per year). Why hasn’t that been done instead of using the leak as a major talking point in the campaign?
articles.title: Measure UU and some comprehensive solutions

articles.text: Prior to Covid I swam 3-5 days per week, so I like pools. But I am voting No on Measure UU. I don’t like being duped. The bond for replacing the pool was rushed on to this year’s ballot because the City feared that if they asked for what was really needed, $70 million to upgrade the police and fire buildings, which includes the pool, that voters would reject it. It was too much money to ask at one time and the City knew this. So instead, it was decided to slip Measure UU in knowing the psychology of asking for a smaller amount now, knowing that voters would vote later on the estimated $50 million needed to upgrade the fire and police buildings, which I support. What galls me is that the true cost of building a new pool is not known. The City Council passed a $23 million ordinance for improvements yet approved a $19.5 million bond measure for the ballot. I am advocating to vote No on Measure UU and have the City to do the job right, which is to get the proper cost estimates. We are entitled to know how our money will be spent. Use logic and don’t be persuaded by fear tactics.

No for now on UU By Sam Smith Editor: I think without question we need a new pool facility in the center of Piedmont. There have been pleas from parents, grandparents, water polo team members and realtors stating that it is an important amenity to have in this town. As Alan Rudy, an experienced architect and longstanding resident said, this needs more study. We need to prioritize with police and fire safety, and the general upkeep of our town. Not so fast, Piedmont. Nobody is against a pool. Every town needs a local swimming hole. However, these are the reasons why we are voting No on UU at this time: Overdone ask: The analysis shows that the current facility can be replaced for approximately $10 million. The committee wants a blank check with flexibility to build the Hearst Castle of pools. Replace what we have with new and safe facilities, but don’t ask to develop additional buildings and a facility that goes beyond what we need. The UU committee says that non-residents will help pay the operational bill with entrance fees. Why aren’t we building something that can be self-sustained vs. something that only works with outside revenue dependence? Unfair taxing approach: The independent tax report done earlier this year said taxes for such amenities should be done using the parcel tax approach, not the ad valorem methodology. The marketing campaign for UU quotes average taxes on a daily basis. This is highly misleading. In fact, the tax report shows that 20% of the homes would pay 50% of the tax. The 20% are our newer homeowners, many with young families and dual-working parents. This just isn’t fair to them. Too quick: The whole plan has been rushed and put together too fast under the guise that the pool is not functional. There just hasn’t been enough study. Sure, the pool is leaking. Close it down, get a more concrete plan in place and come to the voters in a special election when ready and have us decide. Piedmont, please, No on UU. This is too much too quick. Andersen wants us to be thoughtful By Andy Wasserman In the recent LWV Forum on Measure UU reported on by the Post, Betsy Andersen was asked why the Council is prioritizing the pool over public services buildings. She replied that she does not see Measure UU as a choice between the two, but that “our community can and should thoughtfully do both”. Seriously? Of course it is a choice. By rushing through UU before it asks for even more money for essential services, the council is clearly prioritizing the pool. Stop and think – what are your priorities? Having Police and Fire Services that comply with state law and having facilities that do not collapse in an earthquake, or a swimming pool? Does anyone really think there is a choice? The total cost to repay $19.5 million in 30-year bonds at 3% interest is $29.6 million. The total cost to repay the $51 million of bonds it will take to rebuild the Police and Fire Stations with the same assumptions is $77.4 million. That’s a total of $107 million for the two projects. The City Council has admitted that it needs to do the essential services upgrade, both to comply with current law and to be able to provide services in case of a natural disaster. Let’s be “thoughtful”, as Ms. Andersen suggests, and put the pool on hold until the City’s essential services problems have been fixed. Then see if people still have the appetite and the financial resources for a pool. articles.text: The updated schedule for the revised reopening of elementary schools, approved by the school board on Monday night this week, October 26. restrictions Alameda County has permission from the state to open all schools. Alameda County’s Public Health Office enacted tighter restrictions which allowed for only elementary schools to open starting October 13 with a public reopening plan. Piedmont was slated to be the first public school in the county to reopen. Many private schools in the county already opened up this month. Middle schools in Alameda County do not have the green light to open now, and mid-November is expected to be the earliest date for them. High schools are not expected to be given the opportunity to open until next year, possibly in January 2021. While older students are more likely to be able to follow distancing and mask wearing rules, they are thought to transmit SARSCOV-2 more easily than the youngest learners. Many frustrated parents called into the three-hour special meeting on Monday night to voice their grievances, offer suggestions and query school board members. In an emotionally charged call to the board, Piedmont parent Laura Maestrelli read off nearly 10 anonymous responses from PHS and PMS students negatively affected by Distance Learning. “Every day feels the exact the same. I get headaches because of class and homework on screens. I have lost all motivation. It feels like we have whittled it down to the most depressing and worst parts of school – and that’s all we are doing,” said a PHS freshman. Many parents calling in expressed helplessness. Booker suggested some options for them. “The number one way [to help] is pay attention to the social contract. It only works if we all [follow those safety requirements]. Families have to do the health screening every morning, that is really important. We will be asking for help to grab some materials, like clorox wipes, and hand sanitizer,” Booker said. The reopening plan for TK-K still consists of only 2-hours, 15-minutes of in-person instruction four days a week, Tuesday through Friday. All elementary students have distance learning on Mondays. Grades 1-5 will have an additional 45 minutes of instruction. Classes have been split into AM and PM cohorts, with a maximum of 15 students per cohort. The schedules for distance learning and in-person learning are the same as they have been all year. Specialist instruction (P.E, art, computers) will be taught digitally, 45 minutes per day for TK - K and an hour for grades 1-5. Expanding the duration of instruction and giving parents the option to switch to in-person learning will take place later in the year, after scheduled breaks from instruction. An idea floated around the meeting about a rolling reopening to start sooner than December 1 for classes that do have teacher assignments lined up. Booker worried that parents would be upset if in-person school started for some kids, but not for others. Board member Cory Smegal recommended reflecting these parent’s desire. The board approved the motion to “Direct the superintendent to explore having a trial to bring a small number of general education students back prior to Thanksgiving break.” The most acute special education learners will return to campus November 3 at elementary schools as planned. Middle schools in Alameda County do not have the green light to open now, and mid-November is expected to be the earliest date for them. High schools are not expected to be given the opportunity to open until next year, possibly in January 2021. While older students are more likely to be able to follow distancing and mask wearing rules, they are thought to transmit SARSCOV-2 more easily than the youngest learners. Many frustrated parents called into the three-hour special meeting on Monday night to voice their grievances, offer suggestions and query school board members. In an emotionally charged call to the board, Piedmont parent Laura Maestrelli read off nearly 10 anonymous responses from PHS and PMS students negatively affected by Distance Learning. “Every day feels the exact the same. I get headaches because of class and homework on screens. I have lost all motivation. It feels like we have whittled it down to the most depressing and worst parts of school – and that’s all we are doing,” said a PHS freshman. Many parents calling in expressed helplessness. Booker suggested some options for them. “The number one way [to help] is pay attention to the social contract. It only works if we all [follow those safety requirements]. articles.text: Residents advised to prepare for wildfire and power outages – again Hurricane force gusts blew through the North Bay this past weekend, and the entire Bay Area, including Piedmont, was put under a Red Flag Warning on Sunday, October 25. While the warning was lifted for Piedmont earlier this week, the Red Flag Warning persisted until 5 p.m. yesterday, Tuesday, October 27 for the East Bay Hills and North Bay Mountains. Dangerous wildfire weather is expected in the near term, so vigilance amongst the public is paramount, Fire Chief Bret Black explained. High winds and low humidity in the forecast are behind the concerns. “We are under extreme weather conditions ripe for a significant wildfire,” Black noted. On Monday, October 26, the National Weather Service measured peak wind gusts of 89 miles per hour, which counts as hurricane force, in the Mayacmas Mountains in the North Bay. That day at Mt. Diablo to the east of Piedmont, 70 miles per hour gusts were recorded. The NWS measured gusts over 50 miles per hour in Piedmont, where winds knocked down tree branches. But the temperatures remained cool, not the hot winds associated with fire-inducing winds from the East. “The low humidity and wind are posing a significant risk to all Californians,” Black said. A 2-alarm fire in Montclair yesterday, October 27, caused damage to two homes. PFD Fire Crew sent to So. Calif. The Piedmont Fire Department sent an engine down this week to fight devastating fires burning in Southern California. The PFD engine was sent along with 10 engines from other local agencies to battle the Silverado Fire near Irvine. Yesterday, Black noted that a fire in the Oakland neighborhood of Montclair ignited two homes and some vegetation. The Oakland Fire Department said no one was hurt but eight people were displaced. “Luckily, we have additional engines staged in the vicinity and the fire was quickly brought under control,” said Black, adding that it took several hours to extinguish all the small hot spots in the area. Tens of thousands of PG&E customers in the Bay Area were without power during a portion of the weekend due to a Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) due to the high fire danger. Some homes on the eastern edge of Piedmont were impacted on Sunday, October 25, and as of yesterday, several dozen customers in the City reported a loss of power. CalFire notes that “wildfire season” will last for several more weeks. Some of the most devastating wildfires in California history, such as the 2018 Camp Fire, began in November. The Piedmont Fire Department encourages all residents to prepare for fire emergencies. Black recommends Piedmonters learn how to prevent wildfires by visiting the PFD webpage of the City’s website and www.ReadyForWildfire.org.

A 24-hour accessible ballot drop-box is located on Highland Way and Highland Avenue in Piedmont. “We’ve been preparing for this,” Alameda County Registrar of Voters Information Officer Tim Dupuis said, adding that his department has doubled availability to match the record number of voters this year. Piedmont, a city already noted as producing the highest percentage of voters per capita in Alameda County, is also expected to show a record number of votes cast this year. Piedmont set a new county record in 2016 with an 86-percent voter turnout based upon 8,634 registered voters. The city’s current number of registered voters has increased to 9,035. The city’s population is 11,400. A nationwide “Walk the Vote” event, a grassroots effort aimed on promoting the importance of voting, was originally planned for Piedmont this weekend. It was then cancelled because of the high number of votes already placed. “After much back and forth with the [organizers] and Walk A Vote by Mail drop box is located on Highland Way and Highland Avenue outside the Wells Fargo building. the Vote team, we have found that there may not be a need for a walk in Piedmont, as an overwhelming majority of the residents have already voted – which is great,” Walk the Vote organizer Michael Stouber said. Yesterday was the last day to request a Vote by Mail Ballot for the November 3 General Election, but you can still vote early in person. “If anyone wants to vote early right now, even if they don’t have their ballot, they can come to our main office in downtown Oakland in the courthouse, and they can come and get their ballot and vote it,” Dupuis said.

articles.text: Led by Lt. Justin McNulty, a four-man strike team from Piedmont Fire Department left Tuesday morning, October 27, for Orange County in Southern California to assist in containing the Silverado Fire near Irvine. The crew that departed yesterday at 8:30 a.m. includes Engineer Alan Grace, Firefighter Sandor Lengyel, and Firefighter-Paramedic Brian Gidney. Piedmont Fire Chief Bret Black said that he expects the crew to be there through the weekend. The Silverado Fire began on Monday, October 26, in eastern Orange County and quickly spread west, forcing evacuations in Irvine. About 91,000 residents have been evacuated as of Tuesday afternoon. The fire is situated around Santiago Canyon Road and Silverado Canyon Road, southwest of Silverado. The fire may have been caused by Southern California Edison equipment, the utility company said late Monday. Edison officials in a letter to the California Public Utilities Commission said, “Preliminary information reflects SCE (Southern California Edison) overhead electrical facilities are located in the origin area of the Silverado Fire. We have no indication of any circuit activity prior to the reported time of the fire, nor downed overhead primary conductors in the origin area. However, it appears that a lashing wire that was attached to an underbuilt telecommunication line may have contacted SCE’s overhead primary conductor which may have resulted in the ignition of the fire. The investigation is ongoing.” Historically, October is one of the most destructive months of the year for wildfires in California, due in large part to months of dry conditions and strong winds. That has shifted in recent years, though, and especially in 2020. This year, the largest and most destructive wildfires in Northern California have occurred in August and September.

pages.text: 32 Wednesday, October 28, 2020 Hurricane-type wind recorded in North Bay Residents advised to prepare for wildfire and power outages – again By Barry Eitel Hurricane force gusts blew through the North Bay this past weekend, and the entire Bay Area, including Piedmont, was put under a Red Flag Warning on Sunday, October 25. While the warning was lifted for Piedmont earlier this week, the Red Flag Warning persisted until 5 p.m. yesterday, Tuesday, October 27 for the East Bay Hills and North Bay Mountains. Dangerous wildfire weather is expected in the near term, so vigilance amongst the public is paramount, Fire Chief Bret Black explained. High winds and low humidity in the forecast are behind the concerns. “We are under extreme weather conditions ripe for a significant wildfire,” Black noted. On Monday, October 26, the National Weather Service measured peak wind gusts of 89 miles per hour, which counts as hurricane force, in the Mayacmas Mountains in the North Bay. That day at Mt. Diablo to the east of Piedmont, 70 miles per hour gusts were recorded. The NWS measured gusts over 50 miles per hour in Piedmont, where winds knocked down tree branches. But the temperatures remained cool, not the hot winds associated with fire-inducing winds from the East. “The low humidity and wind are posing a significant risk to all Californians,” Black said. A 2-alarm fire in Montclair yesterday, October 27, caused damage to two homes. PFD Fire Crew sent to So. Calif. The Piedmont Fire Department sent an engine down this week to fight devastating fires burning in Southern California. The PFD engine was sent along with 10 engines from other local agencies to battle the Silverado Fire near Irvine. Yesterday, Black noted that a fire in the Oakland neighborhood of Montclair ignited two homes and some vegetation. The Oakland Fire Department said no one was hurt but eight people were displaced. “Luckily, we have additional engines staged in the vicinity and the fire was quickly brought under control,” said Black, adding that it took several hours to extinguish all the small hot spots in the area. Tens of thousands of PG&E customers in the Bay Area were without power during a portion of the weekend due to a Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) due to the high fire danger. Some homes on the eastern edge of Piedmont were impacted on Sunday, October 25, and as of yesterday, several dozen customers in the City reported a loss of power. CalFire notes that “wildfire season” will last for several more weeks. Some of the most devastating wildfires in California history, such as the 2018 Camp Fire, began in November. The Piedmont Fire Department encourages all residents to prepare for fire emergencies. Black recommends Piedmonters learn how to prevent wildfires by visiting the PFD webpage of the City’s website and www.ReadyForWildfire.org. Piedmont firefighters helping at Silverado fire in SoCal By Allyson Aleksey Led by Lt. Justin McNulty, a four-man strike team from Piedmont Fire Department left Tuesday morning, October 27, for Orange County in Southern California to assist in containing the Silverado Fire near Irvine. The crew that departed yesterday at 8:30 a.m. includes Engineer Alan Grace, Firefighter Sandor Lengyel, and Firefighter-Paramedic Brian Gidney. Piedmont Fire Chief Bret Black said that he expects the crew to be there through the weekend. The Silverado Fire began on Monday, October 26, in eastern Orange County and quickly spread west, forcing evacuations in Irvine. About 91,000 residents have been evacuated as of Tuesday afternoon. The fire is situated around Santiago Canyon Road and Silverado Canyon Road, southwest of Silverado. The fire may have been caused by Southern California Edison equipment, the utility company said late Monday. Edison officials in a letter to the California Public Utilities Commission said, “Preliminary information reflects SCE (Southern California Edison) overhead electrical facilities are located in the origin area of the Silverado Fire. We have no indication of any circuit activity prior to the reported time of the fire, nor downed overhead primary conductors in the origin area. However, it appears that a lashing wire that was attached to an underbuilt telecommunication line may have contacted SCE’s overhead primary conductor which may have resulted in the ignition of the fire. The investigation is ongoing.” Historically, October is one of the most destructive months of the year for wildfires in California, due in large part to months of dry conditions and strong winds. That has shifted in recent years, though, and especially in 2020. This year, the largest and most destructive wildfires in Northern California have occurred in August and September. 2020 Calendar of Events October 21 - November 3 Meetings will be conducted by ZOOM and should be viewable on KCOM (Channel 27) and on the City’s website: piedmont.ca.gov. By comparison, the county only had 28 vote-by-mail drop boxes for the mid-term election in 2018. A 24-hour accessible ballot drop-box is located on Highland Way and Highland Avenue in Piedmont. “We’ve been preparing for this,” Alameda County Registrar of Voters Information Officer Tim Dupuis said, adding that his department has doubled availability to match the record number of voters this year. Piedmont, a city already noted as producing the highest percentage of voters per capita in Alameda County, is also expected to show a record number of votes cast this year. Piedmont set a new county record in 2016 with an 86-percent voter turnout based upon 8,634 registered voters. The city’s current number of registered voters has increased to 9,035. The city’s population is 11,400. A nationwide “Walk the Vote” event, a grassroots effort aimed on promoting the importance of voting, was originally planned for Piedmont this weekend. It was then cancelled because of the high number of votes already placed. “After much back and forth with the [organizers] and Walk A Vote by Mail drop box is located on Highland Way and Highland Avenue outside the Wells Fargo building. the Vote team, we have found that there may not be a need for a walk in Piedmont, as an overwhelming majority of the residents have already voted – which is great,” Walk the Vote organizer Michael Stouber said. Yesterday was the last day to request a Vote by Mail Ballot for the November 3 General Election, but you can still vote early in person. “If anyone wants to vote early right now, even if they don’t have their ballot, they can come to our main office in downtown Oakland in the courthouse, and they can come and get their ballot and vote it,” Dupuis said. Where in the World Are We? Jack Miller, a 4th grader at Havens School, and brother Sam, a second grader, recently got to head to New York City during a school break. While there they headed to New York’s Hudson Yards where they toured The Vessel, an elaborate honeycomb-like structure rises 16 stories and consists of 154 flights of stairs, 2,500 steps, and 80 landings for visitors to climb. articles.title: Proud Supporters of Measure UU - Join Us!

pages.text: YES on Measure UU Dear Piedmont Community, With the election less than a week away, we want to express our appreciation for the thousands of hours spent by hundreds of volunteers working hard to pass Measure UU for the future of Piedmont. It’s inspiring to see citizens of all ages and backgrounds reaching out to friends and neighbors to talk about the need to replace the failing Piedmont Pool. When the three of us stepped up to lead this campaign, we had no idea that we would be supported by such a diverse and talented team, including community leaders, neighborhood advocates, students -- athletes and non-athletes, and over 600 community endorsers. Like us, they are motivated by the fact that the Piedmont Pool has been an integral part of our community and our schools for 56 years. Their enthusiasm and efforts to bring people together and strengthen our community reflect the very best of Piedmont. Please join all of us and vote Yes on Measure UU! Amy Aubrecht, Anne Callahan & Vince Saunders Co-Chairs, Community Pool for Piedmont - Yes on Measure UU Proud Supporters of Measure UU - Join Us!
